lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the B-1147 recall at HealthTrade
lessons.html:
This chapter runs the Chapter 7 procedure on a real morning. Values and timings are listed per step.

The trigger. A regulator's letter arrives at 08:40 on a Tuesday: a manufacturer-level quality recall naming PARA-500, batch B-1147.

Step 1 — freeze, 08:40-08:55. The stock manager opens Batch B-1147 — one search, because receiving discipline stored the manufacturer's own number — and sets Disabled. All three sites see the block at once: the Ibadan till's attempt to sell a strip of the batch at 09:10 is refused by the system before the branch has finished reading the notification message. The keeper message goes out at 08:52 naming the item, the batch, and the segregation instruction. Notice-to-freeze: fifteen minutes.

Step 2 — locate, by 09:05. The batch-wise balance prints the network snapshot: 34 cartons at Central, 12 at Ibadan, 0 at Akure (Akure's PARA-500 stock was always a different lot — the batch balance proves it in one line, sparing Akure the shelf sweep), 0 in transit. The snapshot files as page one.

Step 3 — quarantine, same morning. Central: one transfer, 34 cartons to Central - Quarantine, shelf-checked. Ibadan: 12 cartons to a segregated, labelled area per the branch procedure and transferred in the system to the quarantine designation the site uses. Both transfers file as custody evidence.

Step 4 — the downstream trace, same day.

1. The delivery and sales documents citing B-1147 list the wholesale customers who received the batch and the quantities; the notification list builds from it and goes out per the letter's instruction.
2. The produced-from trace: module 2's repack register shows the standing carton-to-strip conversion, and the repack entries citing B-1147 account for 88 retail strips at Central produced from the batch — the strips inherit the recall, are located by the same batch balance (the inheritance discipline paying at the exact moment it exists for), and join the quarantine transfer.
3. Returns: two wholesale customers return their holdings over the following week, received into quarantine against the notification list.

Step 5 — the account. The final disposition per the manufacturer's instruction: the quarantined stock returns to the manufacturer, documented through the return flow with the batch named, the credit handled by the Procurement track's lanes. The recall file closes: notice, timings, snapshot, transfers, trace, notification list, returns, disposition — one folder, and the regulator's follow-up inspection three weeks later is answered from it in one sitting.

The findings, flat. Two process notes from the live run, both fixed within the week: the Ibadan keeper message went to the keeper's personal line rather than the duty channel (the notification list on the procedure corrected to the duty channel); and one wholesale delivery from the trace pre-dated batch capture on that customer's document type (a configuration gap from the go-live era — the affected document class confirmed batch-mandatory, and the customer contacted from the receipt-date range instead). The drill calendar adopts the real run's timings as its baseline: fifteen minutes to freeze, twenty-five to located.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in identity operations, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — system batches over manufacturer lots. Symptom: auto-created batch numbers on regulated goods; a recall letter naming a number the system has never heard of; the freeze step becoming a research project. Correction: the posture switched to manual capture; existing lots re-identified by remediation where feasible. Prevention: the control register's posture per class — manual manufacturer numbers wherever a recall can name them.

Error 2 — expiry from the packing list. Symptom: expiry dates entered from paperwork rather than labels; the expiry reads mis-scheduled for the life of every mis-entered lot. Correction: the identity audit re-checking labels against Batch records; corrections documented. Prevention: the dock rule — dates from the printed label, confirmed by the second signature.

Error 3 — identity unconfirmed at handover. Symptom: transfers received on quantity alone; batch balances wrong at both sites while totals reconcile. Correction: the affected batches recounted per site and corrected by document. Prevention: the receiving procedure's explicit batch comparison — identity, not just quantity.

Error 4 — the broken inheritance. Symptom: repacks producing anonymous or new batches; the recall trace stopping at the conversion; retail stock unreachable by the lot that made it. Correction: produced batches re-linked to sources where records allow; the register's inheritance rule enforced. Prevention: module 2's conversion register carrying the batch handling per conversion, and the monthly repack read checking it.

Error 5 — the paper procedure. Symptom: a recall procedure that exists as a document and has never run; the first live recall spent learning the tools. Correction: the drill run now. Prevention: the twice-yearly drill with recorded timings and source-fixed findings.

Error 6 — expired stock on the shelf. Symptom: the expired list carrying aged lines; expired goods pickable; write-offs discovered rather than decided. Correction: the expired lane run — quarantine, write-off with approvals, disposal per compliance. Prevention: the weekly expired read at target zero and the 90-day working list feeding the near-expiry lanes in time.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the two identities and what each buys; configure an item from the control register — batch posture, expiry, shelf life, serials, warranty — and state why flags precede stock; create and read Batch records, the batch-wise balance, and the bundle mechanics including multi-batch rows and first-expiry-first-out; operate Serial No capture at receipt, verification at delivery, and the location census; run every movement with identity — the dock discipline, transfer confirmation, per-batch issues, repack inheritance, delivery bundles, per-batch counts; run the expiry reads and lanes on their cadences; and execute the recall procedure to its time targets with the drill.

Module rule 3: identity travels with the stock — captured once from the physical goods at the dock, named on every movement and confirmed at every handover, expiries read on their horizons, and any batch freezable and locatable across the network in minutes. Module 4 covers stock reconciliation and counting.

counting.title: Inventory 4 — Stock Reconciliation & Counting
counting.desc: Stock reconciliation and counting in ZhiftERP: the Stock Reconciliation field walk — the two purposes, the set-to rule, the valuation-rate caution, the Difference Account, and what submission posts; count preparation with cut-off, the freeze setting, blind numbered sheets, and team separations; the floor rules including the double-count pass and the during-count procedure; entry, the recount pass, the threshold ladder, and the keeper review; the variance investigation — the document sweep first, the physical causes, the loss finding with the pattern file, and the upstream fix; and ABC cycle counting with the daily slice and the accuracy metric.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Counting: scope and instruments
lessons.html:
This module covers stock counting and the Stock Reconciliation in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Stock Reconciliation field walk and state what submission posts; prepare a count with cut-off, freeze, and blind sheets; execute the physical count with its team rules; enter results and run the variance review with its threshold ladder; investigate variances to their causes before adjusting; and operate ABC cycle counting with the accuracy metric.

Why counts exist. The records say what should be on the shelf; the count establishes what is. The difference — the variance — is information: a missing document, a process gap, a loss. Counting is not suspicion of the keepers; it is the periodic proof of custody the keepers themselves rely on, and the module's controls protect the counters as much as the stock.

The two instruments.

1. The count procedure — the human process: preparation, blind sheets, teams, execution, review (Chapters 3-5). The procedure produces a verified physical truth.
2. The Stock Reconciliation — the document that aligns the records to the verified truth (Chapter 2). It is the last step, never the first: an adjustment posted before investigation converts information into silence.

The count types.

1. The full count — every line in a warehouse (or the business), typically annual, often with the external auditor observing per the Accounts track's year-end.
2. The cycle count — a rotating slice counted on a calendar, weighted by value (Chapter 7's ABC design). The cycle count is the working control: small daily effort, continuous accuracy evidence.
3. The spot count — unannounced, targeted: a variance pattern, an incident, a handover. Ordered by the stock manager or owner; same procedure at small scale.

Custody and the separations. Module 1's rule operates throughout: the keeper participates in counting but does not approve their own adjustments; sheets are blind (no system quantities shown); the counter and the enterer verify each other through the signed sheet; adjustments post under Stock Manager authority per the value ladder (Chapter 5). No single person can hold the stock, count it, and rewrite its record.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Stock Reconciliation doctype. Chapter 3: count preparation. Chapter 4: executing the count. Chapter 5: entry and the variance review. Chapter 6: the variance investigation. Chapter 7: ABC cycle counting. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Stock Reconciliation doctype
lessons.html:
Open Stock Reconciliation (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order, and know what submission posts before ever submitting one.

1. Purpose. Two values:

• Stock Reconciliation — the standing purpose: aligning existing records to a count.
• Opening Stock — the implementation-era purpose: loading opening balances at go-live, with opening rates from the accountant's verified costing (the go-live procedure's territory; the rate check against recent purchase documents is part of it, because an opening rate wrong by a factor propagates into every valuation after it).

2. Posting Date and Time. The count's cut-off moment (Chapter 3) — the reconciliation posts as of the instant the physical truth was established, which is what makes the comparison honest.

3. The Items table. One row per counted line:

• Item Code and Warehouse — the pair being aligned.
• Qty — the verified physical quantity. A row with quantity entered sets the balance to that figure (not by that figure): the reconciliation states the truth, and the system computes the difference itself.
• Valuation Rate — normally left to the current ledger rate; entered only when the reconciliation is deliberately revaluing (the accountant's decision, documented — module 5 covers valuation corrections). A rate typed casually here is a valuation event typed casually.
• Batch / serial handling — controlled items reconcile per batch (module 3's per-batch counting), the rows carrying their identity.
• The fetch tools pull current system quantities into the table for the counted scope — used at entry time to build the comparison, never printed onto count sheets (the blind rule, Chapter 3).

4. The Difference Account. The account the value delta posts to — the stock adjustment account the chart provides, per the accountant's design. The account is set deliberately; the reconciliation's value effect is an accounting entry like any other and lands where the chart says shrinkage and count adjustments live.

5. What submission posts. Per row where the entered quantity differs from the system's: a Stock Ledger Entry adjusting the balance to the stated figure, and the value difference posting between the stock account and the Difference Account. In one sentence: a Stock Reconciliation moves real value with one document — and for this reason it sits behind the Stock Manager role, the draft review, and the approval ladder, and why every row above the investigation threshold carries its investigation reference (Chapter 6) before submission.

6. Scope discipline. One reconciliation per counted scope (a warehouse, a cycle slice), rows limited to what was actually counted. The reconciliation that includes uncounted lines to tidy them adjusts records against no physical truth — the exact inversion of the instrument's purpose.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Count preparation
lessons.html:
A count's quality is decided before anyone touches a shelf. This chapter is the preparation procedure.

1. Scope and schedule. Define the scope (the warehouse, or the cycle slice per Chapter 7's calendar) and the date. Full counts are scheduled clear of peak trading and announced to operations — the count competes with the work otherwise; cycle counts run on their standing calendar; spot counts are unannounced by design.

2. The cut-off. The count compares shelf to records as of one moment. Two ways to hold the moment:

1. Movements stopped — for full counts: receiving, despatch, and issues for the scope pause for the count window; documents in flight are completed or excluded explicitly (the transit warehouse holds the in-motion stock cleanly, per module 2's design).
2. The freeze setting — Stock Settings carries the stock-freeze controls: postings dated up to the freeze date are blocked for ordinary roles, with the authorised role named for exceptions. Set the freeze for full counts and year-end; the exception role is held per the sysadmin matrix and every exceptional posting during a freeze carries its reason.

3. Pre-count hygiene. The week before a full count:

1. Open documents for the scope cleared: drafts submitted or deleted, transit lines received or investigated (the count must not discover what the weekly reads should have), pending returns processed.
2. The physical area prepared: stock in its locations, damaged goods already in quarantine by document, unlabelled items resolved.
3. The identity audit prepared for controlled lines (module 3): batch labels checkable against records during the count.

4. The blind sheets. Count sheets print the item lines for the scope — item, description, unit, batch lines for controlled items — without system quantities. The blind rule is the count's core control: a counter who can see the expected figure confirms it; a counter who cannot must establish it. Sheets are numbered, issued per area, and every sheet returns signed — issued-versus-returned is the completeness check.

5. The teams.

1. Counter and checker — two people per area: one counts, one records and verifies. The keeper joins the counting (nobody knows the stock better) but per Chapter 1's separation is never the sole counter of their own custody and never the enterer of their own results.
2. The coordinator — the stock manager or delegate: issues sheets, resolves questions during the count, receives signed sheets, owns the entry and review stages.
3. The auditor's seat — at year-end full counts, the external auditor observes per their procedures; their test counts are facilitated, not shadowed.

6. The briefing. Fifteen minutes before start: the scope, the sheet procedure, the counting unit per line (cartons versus strips — the UoM confusion is the most common count error and the briefing names the unit column explicitly), the damaged-goods rule (found damage is listed and left in place for the document lane, not shuffled off-scope), and the question route to the coordinator.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Executing the count
lessons.html:
The physical procedure, stated as rules the teams follow on the floor.

1. Count what is there. The sheet records the physical quantity found, in the sheet's stated unit, per line and per batch line for controlled items. Rules:

1. Count, do not infer: sealed cartons are counted as cartons only where the policy accepts seal integrity (and the policy says which classes; high-value and regulated classes open per the sampling rule); part cartons are opened and counted in units.
2. The unit column governs: every figure is written in the line's stated unit. A count written in strips against a carton line is the error the briefing warned about; the checker's job is exactly this verification.
3. Location sweep: the team counts the area, not the list — stock found that is not on the sheet is written onto the sheet's exceptions section with its location (unlisted stock is either mis-shelved, mis-scoped, or a receiving bypass, and each is worth knowing).
4. Identity riding along (module 3): batch numbers and expiry labels checked against the sheet's batch lines; disagreements noted on the line — the count is the identity audit's vehicle.

2. Damage and condition. Found damage is recorded on the line's note and the goods left in place: the damage lane (module 2, Chapter 3) runs by document after the count, with the count note as part of its evidence. The count establishes quantity and condition; it does not execute disposals.

3. The double-count rule. Lines the coordinator designates — high value, historically variant, or randomly sampled per the policy's percentage — are counted independently by a second team before sheets return. Two independent physical figures that agree are the strongest truth the count can produce; where they disagree, the line is counted a third time with the coordinator present.

4. Sheet discipline.

1. Figures in ink, corrections struck through and initialled — the sheet is the count's primary evidence and it must read as what happened.
2. Both team members sign each sheet; the keeper's signature joins for their custody's sheets (the keeper attests the count happened over their stock; the separation rules govern what happens next, not whether they participate).
3. Sheets return to the coordinator as areas complete; the issued-versus-returned check closes before anyone leaves.

5. During-count movements. Where an unavoidable movement must happen inside the window (the emergency despatch the business cannot refuse), the coordinator executes it explicitly: the affected lines re-counted after, the movement documented with its during-count flag, the reconciliation's cut-off arithmetic told about it. An undocumented mid-count movement invalidates every affected line silently — the one thing the procedure cannot survive.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Entry and the variance review
lessons.html:
The counted truth meets the records. This chapter is the entry procedure and the review that decides what posts.

1. Entry. The coordinator's team enters the sheets: the counted quantities per line into the working comparison (the reconciliation draft's fetch tools pulling system figures beside them — Chapter 2). Entry rules:

1. The enterer works from signed sheets only, and is not the counter of the lines being entered (the separation completing its loop).
2. Entry is checked line-for-line against the sheets by a second person for full counts; sampled for cycle counts per the policy.
3. The exceptions section (unlisted stock) enters as its own list for Chapter 6's lanes.

2. The variance report. The comparison produces, per line: system quantity, counted quantity, variance in units, variance in value (at the ledger's valuation rate). Sort by absolute value — the review works the money, not the row count.

3. The recount pass. Before any investigation: every line above the recount threshold (the policy's figure) is physically recounted by a fresh team against the specific line. Recounts kill the cheap causes first — the transcription slip, the missed second location, the unit error — and the variance that survives recount is real information worth Chapter 6's effort. The recount result replaces the count figure on the working comparison with its own initialled sheet note.

4. The threshold ladder. The written policy sets the bands; the standing shape:

1. Below the de-minimis band — small variances post on the reconciliation with the count as their evidence, batched, reviewed as a total (the total's trend is Chapter 7's accuracy metric in value form).
2. The investigation band — lines above it do not post until Chapter 6's investigation attaches its outcome reference to the row.
3. The escalation band — lines above it go to the owner with the investigation, because a variance of that size is a business event, not a stock adjustment.

5. The posting. One Stock Reconciliation per scope (Chapter 2's discipline): rows for the verified lines, quantities set to counted truth, the Difference Account per the chart, investigation references on every banded row, the draft reviewed by the second authority, submitted under Stock Manager per the ladder. The signed sheets, the variance report, and the investigation notes attach to the reconciliation — the count answers from one document set, per the standing one-lookup standard.

6. The keeper conversation. The scope's keeper sees the variance report before posting and signs the reconciliation's review: their custody, their right to explain, and their attestation that the process ran fairly. The count that posts adjustments behind the keeper's back has traded a control for a grievance.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The variance investigation
lessons.html:
A variance that survives recount is a question with a findable answer. This chapter is the investigation procedure and its outcome lanes.

1. The document sweep — always first. Most real variances are paperwork, and the sweep finds them in this order:

1. The unposted movement — the despatch physically gone but never entered, the receipt shelved but never posted: the item's recent physical events walked against its ledger. The stock entry drafts, the pending purchase and delivery documents for the item, and the branch's paper trail all check here.
2. The transit and boundary check — stock counted at neither end because it sits in transit (correctly — the count's scope arithmetic verifies it) or incorrectly (module 2's shortfall lane never run).
3. The pending-document check — submitted orders awaiting receipt entry, returns awaiting processing: the movement exists in intent, the posting lagged.
4. The timing check — a movement posted after the cut-off but performed before it (or the reverse): the cut-off arithmetic corrected, not the stock.

2. The physical causes. Where the documents are whole:

1. The identity confusion — the variance mirrored by an opposite variance on a similar item (the two strengths of the same drug counted into each other's lines): corrected as the pair it is.
2. The UoM arithmetic — carton/unit conversion errors in past postings (module 3's fractional-batch symptom): the causing document found and corrected through the lane.
3. The repack drift — module 2's register comparison for converted items.

3. The loss finding. Where the sweep and the physical causes close nothing, the variance is a loss (or a gain) with no document — and the finding is handled as the business event it is:

1. The write-off (or the found-stock receipt) posts through its lane with the investigation attached, approved per the band — a loss is a decided expense even when its mechanism is unknown.
2. The incident enters the pattern file: item, warehouse, value, date, and whatever the investigation established. One unexplained loss is a data point; the pattern file is where three data points become a shape — the same item class, the same shift window, the same handover — and the shape is what the owner acts on. The file is reviewed quarterly with the counts' accuracy read.
3. Where the pattern or the value indicates it, the security response is the owner's decision, informed by the file — the investigation's job is facts, per the standing data-not-editorial rule.

4. The upstream fix. Every investigation closes with one line: what would have prevented this variance, and which procedure now carries it. The unposted-despatch finding tightens the same-day entry rule at its site; the identity confusion adds the look-alike pair to the count briefing; the timing error adjusts the cut-off procedure. The investigation that only adjusts the number has done half its job; the count exists to improve the process that feeds it.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — ABC cycle counting
lessons.html:
The cycle count converts the annual count's mountain into a daily routine. This chapter is the design and the metric.

1. The ABC classification. Rank the warehouse's items by annual consumption value (or stock value where consumption data is young):

1. A items — the top of the ranking holding the bulk of the value (typically a small fraction of the lines holding most of the money).
2. B items — the middle band.
3. C items — the long tail: many lines, little value.

The classification is computed from the reports (module 7's value analytics), reviewed twice a year, and stored as the item's class field or the count calendar's list — a living output of the data, not a one-time label.

2. The count frequencies. Per the written policy, the standing shape: A items counted most often (monthly or better), B quarterly, C annually or by rotation. The design principle: counting effort follows value at risk. The A-class line miscounted for a quarter is real money moving unwatched; the C-class line can wait for its rotation.

3. The cycle calendar. The frequencies compile into a daily list: a fixed small number of lines per warehouse per day, sequenced so every item meets its frequency across the period. The daily slice runs as a miniature of the full procedure — blind lines, counter and checker, the same entry and variance lanes at small scale — and takes minutes: a control that costs minutes daily is run consistently, while a control that requires a full weekend each quarter is postponed.

4. The accuracy metric. Per cycle period, per warehouse: lines counted correct ÷ lines counted (correct meaning within the de-minimis band), expressed as a percentage, trended. The metric is the count programme's output number:

1. It states record reliability to everyone who plans on the records — purchasing, replenishment, the accountant's stock figure.
2. Its trend evaluates process changes: the receiving fix that lifts accuracy two points has proven itself in the metric.
3. Its per-warehouse comparison directs attention: the site running below the network's accuracy gets the next spot count and the process review, as data.

5. The full count's place. Cycle counting does not retire the full count where policy or the auditor requires one (the year-end count with observation stands per the Accounts track); it makes the full count routine — a confirmation of a figure the cycle programme already evidences, instead of an annual reconstruction. A mature cycle programme's year-end variance report is short, and short is the goal.

6. The cycle count's controls. The full procedure's separations apply daily: blind lines, the keeper never sole-counting their own custody, adjustments through the same ladder. Familiarity is the cycle count's risk — the daily routine drifting into confirmation — and the countermeasures are the random double-count sample and the periodic team rotation, both on the policy page.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade's counting year
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade's first counting year. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the opening baseline. The go-live Stock Reconciliation (purpose Opening Stock) loads the opening balances per warehouse. One check runs before submission: opening valuation rates sampled against recent purchase documents — one line found carrying a rate that disagreed with its latest invoice cost and corrected from the document before the figure could propagate. The opening posts with the accountant's sign-off.

Step 2 — the ABC design (Chapter 7). The first classification computes from six months of consumption data: 62 A items carry 71% of the value at Central; B and C bands set behind them. The cycle calendar compiles to five lines per day per warehouse — A items monthly, B quarterly, C by rotation — briefed to the keepers as a ten-minute daily routine with blind lines and the checker rule.

Step 3 — the cycle in operation (Chapters 3-5 at daily scale). The daily slices run; the de-minimis and investigation bands apply from the written ladder. Quarter one's accuracy computes at 96.8% across the network — adopted as the baseline, trended monthly per warehouse thereafter. Ibadan trails the network by two points in month two; the spot review finds the checker step skipped on busy days; the routine re-briefed, the gap closes in month three.

Step 4 — the variance that survived recount (Chapter 6). A cycle line at Central shows 8 cartons of amoxicillin short; the recount confirms it — a real variance above the investigation band, so the row holds unposted. The document sweep runs: the unposted-movement check finds nothing at first pass; the pending-document check finds it — a supplier receipt from twelve days prior, physically shelved but never posted, its paperwork in a tray (the receiving clerk's leave week; no deputy processed the tray). The correction is the missing document entered on its honest date, not a reconciliation adjustment — the shelf was right and the records were behind. The upstream line closes the loop: the deputy rule added to the receiving procedure, and the finding cross-references module 7's aging read, which had flagged the item's stale movement pattern the same week — two reads converging on one gap.

Step 5 — the identity audit riding the counts (module 3 tie). The batch lines on cycle sheets carry the expiry checks; quarter two's audit finds three labels disagreeing with Batch records — all three traced to one dock week and corrected from labels, with the second-signature rule re-briefed at Central receiving.

Step 6 — the year-end full count (Chapters 3-5 at full scale). Scheduled clear of December trading, freeze set, sheets blind, the auditor observing with facilitated test counts. The variance report runs short — the cycle programme's promise — with the posted reconciliation carrying signed sheets, the variance report, and two investigation references. The keeper signatures close each warehouse's file.

The year's close. The pattern file holds four entries, no shape; the accuracy trend sits above baseline at every site; the year-end reconciliation's value total lands inside the de-minimis expectation. The count programme's numbers go to the MD as one page: accuracy per site, variance value posted per band, the two investigations with their upstream fixes.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in counting, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — adjustment before investigation. Symptom: reconciliations posted straight from the variance report; information converted into silence; the same variances recurring because their causes were never found. Correction: banded rows re-opened where feasible, investigated late. Prevention: the threshold ladder — investigation references on every banded row before submission.

Error 2 — sheets with system quantities. Symptom: counts that confirm the records with suspicious perfection; variances surfacing only at handovers and incidents. Correction: the next count run blind and its results compared honestly. Prevention: the blind rule as the procedure's core control, with the sheet template enforcing it.

Error 3 — the keeper counting alone. Symptom: single-signature sheets; the custody separation collapsed; counts that cannot protect the keeper from suspicion or the stock from loss. Correction: the affected scopes recounted with teams. Prevention: counter-and-checker per area, the keeper never sole counter or enterer of their own custody.

Error 4 — the moving target. Symptom: movements during the count window without the coordinator's procedure; lines invalidated silently; the reconciliation arguing with reality. Correction: affected lines identified and recounted. Prevention: the cut-off held — movements stopped or the freeze set, and the explicit during-count procedure for the unavoidable exception.

Error 5 — the postponed mountain. Symptom: no cycle programme; one all-at-once annual count; accuracy unknown for eleven months of the year. Correction: the ABC design built from the value data, the daily slice started. Prevention: the cycle calendar — minutes daily instead of a weekend quarterly, with the accuracy metric proving it.

Error 6 — the metric nobody reads. Symptom: accuracy computed and filed; sites drifting apart; process changes unevaluated. Correction: the trend rebuilt and reviewed. Prevention: the monthly per-warehouse trend to the stock manager and the quarterly page to the owner — the metric as the programme's output, not its by-product.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the two instruments and why the reconciliation is the last step; complete the Stock Reconciliation walk — purposes, the set-to rule, the valuation-rate caution, the Difference Account, what submission posts, and scope discipline; prepare a count — cut-off, freeze, pre-count hygiene, blind numbered sheets, teams, the briefing; execute with the floor rules — count-do-not-infer, the unit column, the location sweep, identity riding along, the double-count rule, sheet discipline; run entry, the recount pass, the threshold ladder, and the keeper conversation; investigate through the document sweep, the physical causes, the loss finding with the pattern file, and the upstream fix; and design ABC cycle counting with the accuracy metric.

Module rule 4: a count proves custody — blind sheets counted and entered by separate hands, variances recounted then investigated before anything posts, adjustments approved by band with their evidence attached, and accuracy measured on a cycle that costs minutes a day. Module 5 covers valuation and the stock ledger.

valuation.title: Inventory 5 — Valuation & the Stock Ledger
valuation.desc: Valuation and the stock ledger in ZhiftERP: the Stock Ledger Entry column walk and the item-story read; Moving Average and FIFO with the container question worked under each; the four doors rates enter through — purchase receipts with the three-way match, the Landed Cost Voucher with its distribution bases, typed Stock Entry rates, and reconciliation rates — and the one door that does not exist; perpetual postings per document and the monthly stock-to-accounts tie-out at target zero; the repost machinery with its operating rules and the remediation-as-project discipline; and the five rate-error reads including the last-paid drift eye and the opening-rate sample.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Valuation: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers stock valuation and the stock ledger in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: read the Stock Ledger Entry and an item's ledger history; state how Moving Average and FIFO compute and when each applies; trace where valuation rates are born, including landed costs; run the monthly stock-to-accounts tie-out under perpetual inventory; operate around the repost machinery; and run the rate-error reads that stop valuation damage at entry.

What valuation is. Every unit of stock carries a value in the records, and that value moves with the stock: into the business at receipt, between warehouses on transfers, out to cost of goods sold at delivery, to expense accounts on issues. The stock figure on the balance sheet and the cost figure on the profit line are both outputs of this module's machinery — and for this reason valuation errors are accounting errors, and why the custody here is shared: the accountant owns the valuation policy (methods, accounts, revaluation decisions); the stock operator owns the record quality the policy computes on.

The Stock Ledger Entry. Every submitted stock document writes Stock Ledger Entry rows — one per item per warehouse touched. The ledger is the stock system's book of record: the Bin (module 1) is its running total; the reports read it; the accounting postings derive from it. Chapter 2 walks the row.

Perpetual inventory. The site runs perpetual inventory: stock documents post accounting entries as they submit — receipt value to the stock account, delivered cost to cost of goods sold, issue value to the named expense account. The stock records and the general ledger are two views of the same events, and Chapter 5's tie-out proves monthly that they still agree.

The module's standing caution. Quantity errors are visible — a shelf disagrees with a bin and a count finds it. Valuation errors are silent: the quantity is right, the value is wrong, and nothing physical ever disagrees. They surface late, in margins that drift and balance-sheet figures that mislead, and they compound — a wrong rate at receipt prices every issue after it. The module's reads (Chapter 7) exist to catch rate errors at the only low-cost moment: entry.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Stock Ledger Entry walk. Chapter 3: the valuation methods. Chapter 4: where rates are born, including the Landed Cost Voucher. Chapter 5: the perpetual postings and the tie-out. Chapter 6: the repost machinery. Chapter 7: the rate-error reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Stock Ledger Entry
lessons.html:
Open Stock Ledger (awesome bar) — the report over Stock Ledger Entry records — filtered to one item and one warehouse. Read the columns in order; together they tell the item's complete value story.

1. Posting Date and Posting Time. The ledger sorts by these; the running figures below are running in this order. This is why module 2's honest-date rule and the backdating controls matter here: an entry inserted into the past changes every running figure after it (Chapter 6's repost).

2. Voucher Type and Voucher No. The document that wrote the row — the Purchase Receipt, Stock Entry, Delivery Note, or Stock Reconciliation. Every ledger row traces to its document in one click; a ledger question is always answered by opening vouchers, never by guessing.

3. Actual Qty. The row's quantity movement: positive in, negative out.

4. Qty After Transaction. The running balance after this row — the Bin's history, row by row.

5. Incoming Rate. On inward rows: the rate this receipt brought — the purchase cost plus landed costs (Chapter 4), or the typed rate on a Material Receipt, or the reconciliation's rate. This column is where rates are born.

6. Valuation Rate. The item-warehouse pair's carrying rate after this row, per the method (Chapter 3): under Moving Average, the recomputed weighted average; under FIFO, the blended figure the remaining queue implies. Outgoing rows consume at the method's rate — the operator never types an outgoing rate.

7. Stock Value and Stock Value Difference. The running value of the balance, and this row's value movement. The Stock Value Difference is exactly what the row posted to the accounts (Chapter 5) — the column that ties the stock ledger to the general ledger line by line.

Reading an item's story. The standing exercise, five minutes per item: filter the ledger, read top to bottom — the opening row, each receipt lifting quantity and moving the rate, each delivery consuming at the carrying rate, the reconciliation rows from counts. Every question this module handles — why is this item's value X, why did the margin move, what did that count adjustment cost — is answered by this read plus the vouchers behind it. An operator who can narrate one item's ledger can investigate any valuation question the business will ever ask.

The ledger's two disciplines, restated from their modules. The rows are only as honest as their documents (module 2's posting discipline), and the running order is only as stable as the backdating controls (Chapter 6). The ledger itself is never edited — like the Bin it feeds, it is derived from documents, and a wrong ledger row is fixed by correcting its voucher through the document lanes.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The valuation methods
lessons.html:
The method decides how outgoing stock is priced and how the carrying rate moves. Two methods; one decision per item; changes are governed events.

1. Moving Average. The carrying rate is the weighted average of what the balance cost:

1. On receipt: the new rate = (existing value + incoming value) ÷ (existing quantity + incoming quantity). Each receipt pulls the average toward its own rate, in proportion to its size.
2. On issue or delivery: the outgoing units price at the current average. The rate does not change on outgoing rows — only the quantity and value fall together.

The container question, worked. A June container of an item lands at a lower cost than March's dearer one, and the owner asks which container this week's deliveries are consuming. Under Moving Average the answer is: neither and both — the deliveries price at the blended average of everything on hand, so the cheap container lowers the cost of every unit sold after its receipt, in proportion. The ledger's Valuation Rate column shows the average stepping down at the June receipt row; the margin improvement that follows is arithmetic, readable on the ledger, not a matter of which physical carton the picker touched.

2. FIFO. The ledger keeps the receipt lots as a queue; outgoing stock consumes the oldest lot's quantity at the oldest lot's rate, then the next. The carrying value is the sum of the surviving lots. Under FIFO the container question has a literal answer — deliveries consume March's costing until March's quantity is gone, then June's — and cost of sales tracks purchase history in sequence.

3. Choosing, and where the choice lives. The Valuation Method field on the Item record, defaulting from Stock Settings where unset. The choice is the accountant's policy decision, made once per item class and recorded with its reason: Moving Average is the common trading default (simple, self-smoothing, one rate to reason about); FIFO where the business wants cost of sales to track purchase sequence. Physical rotation is a separate matter — module 3's first-expiry-first-out governs which carton the picker takes regardless of which method prices it; the method prices, the picking rule rotates, and the two are independent decisions.

4. Method changes. Changing an item's method mid-history is a governed event with the accountant: it changes how every subsequent posting computes and how any repost recomputes the past, so it follows the change discipline — the written decision, the effective boundary, the impact note — and it is rare by design. The method census (items by method against the policy's class table) rides the annual settings review; a register drifting into mixed methods without decisions is Chapter 9's error, found by this read.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Where rates are born
lessons.html:
Every valuation rate enters the system at one of four doors. Each door has its discipline; every valuation error walked through one of them.

1. The Purchase Receipt. The main door: the receipt's rate comes from the purchase order and invoice (the Procurement track's matching controls), and the received quantity at that rate becomes ledger value. The discipline is the Procurement track's — the three-way match is also a valuation control, because the invoice price it verifies is the rate the stock will carry.

2. The Landed Cost Voucher. Freight, clearing, duties, and insurance are part of what the stock cost. Open Landed Cost Voucher (awesome bar) > New:

1. The purchase receipts table — the receipt(s) whose stock the costs belong to.
2. The taxes and charges table — one row per cost: the expense description, the amount, and the account it was booked to.
3. The distribution basis — the costs allocate across the receipts' items by quantity or by value (amount), per the accountant's ruling for the cost type: freight commonly by quantity or weight-proxy, duty by value.
4. Submission — the items' incoming rates and the stock value revalue upward by the allocated amounts (with the repost machinery recomputing downstream rows where needed), and the expense accounts relieve into stock.

The discipline: the voucher is entered when the costs are known, referencing the actual clearing and freight documents, on every import consignment the policy names. A business that receives at invoice price and expenses the freight separately is under-valuing stock and mis-timing margin — the classic pattern the accountant's stock-margin review eventually surfaces, at which point months of receipts need vouchers.

3. The Stock Entry receipt. Module 2's rule restated: the typed Basic Rate on a Material Receipt is a valuation event, sourced from the document that justifies it. The monthly receipts read (module 2, Chapter 7) is also a valuation read — every typed rate on it was a door this chapter's errors could have walked through.

4. The Stock Reconciliation. Two rate cases: the opening-stock load, where rates come from the accountant's verified costing (module 4, Chapter 2 — and the worked example's opening-rate check exists because a wrong opening rate propagates into everything); and the deliberate revaluation, where the accountant's documented decision changes a carrying rate through a reconciliation row — the only lawful revaluation lane, used rarely, always with its paper.

The one door that does not exist. There is no lawful direct edit to a valuation rate — no field on the Bin, no ledger correction by typing. A wrong rate is fixed by correcting the voucher that set it (the amended receipt, the landed cost voucher that was missed) or by the documented revaluation lane; anything else leaves value that disagrees with its own documents, which is the definition of the damage this module exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Perpetual postings and the monthly tie-out
lessons.html:
Under perpetual inventory the stock documents post their own accounting. This chapter is what posts, and the read that proves the two ledgers still agree.

1. What each document posts. Per the Stock Value Difference of its ledger rows (Chapter 2):

1. Purchase Receipt: stock account up; the received-not-invoiced liability up (cleared by the Purchase Invoice per the Procurement track's flow).
2. Delivery Note / sales: stock account down; cost of goods sold up — the margin's cost side, at the method's rate.
3. Stock Entry Material Issue: stock down; the row's Difference Account up (damage, consumption — module 2's account-is-part-of-the-reason rule is an accounting rule here).
4. Material Receipt: stock up against the named account.
5. Transfers: value moves between warehouse-resolved accounts where the chart splits them (module 1, Chapter 2's account field); under a single stock account, no net posting.
6. Stock Reconciliation: the value delta against the Difference Account (module 4).
7. Landed Cost Voucher: stock up; the cost accounts relieved (Chapter 4).

2. The rule that follows. Because the documents post everything, nobody journals the stock accounts by hand. A manual Journal Entry to a stock account creates a general-ledger figure with no stock ledger behind it — the tie-out below breaks by exactly that amount, and the Accounts track's chart controls should withhold the stock accounts from manual posting per the site's configuration. Where a genuine accounting adjustment is needed, it routes through the accountant's decision and the stock-side document that expresses it.

3. The monthly tie-out. With the close, three figures compared:

1. The stock ledger's value — the Stock Balance report's total value as at the close date.
2. The stock account balance(s) — the general ledger's figure for the stock accounts at the same date.
3. The difference — target zero.

A non-zero difference is investigated to its cause, and the causes are a short list: a manual journal to a stock account (found in the account's ledger by voucher type); a posting made while a repost was mid-flight (Chapter 6); a document posted to a date the other view was already reported at (timing — resolved by re-running both at the same timestamp); or damage from a failed migration or patch (the sysadmin incident lane). The tie-out's evidence — both figures, the difference, the cause note — files with the close per the Accounts track's checklist, and the read is the valuation module's one non-negotiable monthly line: everything else in this module can drift quietly; this number cannot.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The repost machinery
lessons.html:
The ledger's running figures depend on order. When a document enters the past, the system recomputes the future. This chapter is the mechanics and the operating rules.

1. Why reposts exist. A backdated receipt changes what the balance cost from its date forward: under Moving Average every subsequent average is different; under FIFO the queue's composition changes. The system therefore reposts — recomputes the valuation of every affected ledger row after the inserted document — through the Repost Item Valuation mechanism, which queues the recomputation as a background job per affected item-warehouse scope.

2. What triggers a repost. Backdated stock documents (module 2's permissioned lane); cancellations and amendments of past documents; Landed Cost Vouchers landing costs onto past receipts; reconciliation rows into the past. In each case the trigger is the same shape: a value event inserted into an already-computed history.

3. The operating rules.

1. Backdating has a compute cost, not just a permission cost. A document one day back recomputes a day's rows; a document three months back recomputes a quarter's rows for the affected items. This is the technical half of why module 2 made backdating a permissioned exception — the habit of late entry is a habit of continuous historical recomputation.
2. Monitor the queue. The Repost Item Valuation list shows queued, in-progress, completed, and failed jobs. The daily glance (riding the sysadmin track's background-jobs read) confirms nothing is stuck: a failed repost means downstream rows are carrying stale valuations right now — an incident for the sysadmin lane, reprocessed from the failed record, never ignored.
3. Do not stack changes onto an in-flight repost. While a large repost runs, further backdated postings and cancellations into the same scope compound the queue and can interleave with the tie-out (Chapter 5's mid-flight cause). Large corrections are scheduled: entered in a quiet window, the queue watched to completion, the tie-out re-run after.
4. Big remediations are projects. A correction touching months of history across many items (Chapter 8's case) is planned with the accountant and the sysadmin: the scope listed, the before-state captured, the entries made in controlled batches, the queue monitored, the tie-out proven at the end. The same change disciplines the programme applies everywhere — written first, staged, verified — applied to the one operation that literally rewrites the value of the past.

4. The period boundary. The Accounts track's period close is also the repost boundary in practice: a closed period refuses the backdated documents that would trigger reposts into reported figures. The stock operator's part of the close is Chapter 5's tie-out plus the transit and negative reads at zero — the stock ledger handed to the close in a state the close can lock.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The rate-error reads
lessons.html:
Valuation errors are silent (Chapter 1); these reads make them loud at the low-cost moment. Each read is stated with its cadence and its action.

1. The last-paid drift eye — at entry, every receipt. The receiving and invoice-matching step compares the incoming rate against the item's recent rate history (the item dashboard's last purchase figures, or the ledger's recent incoming rates). A rate an order of magnitude off its history — ₦96,000 entered against a ₦9,600 history — is a stopped line and a question: a data-entry slip, a unit confusion (the carton rate typed against a unit line — the UoM family of errors again), or a real price event worth confirming. The check takes five seconds per line and catches the class of error that otherwise prices months of issues wrongly. Where the site configures rate-deviation warnings against the last purchase rate, the tolerance is set with the accountant and the warning is treated as the stop it is.

2. The zero-and-strange-rate read — weekly. The Stock Balance report sorted by valuation rate, both ends:

1. Zero or near-zero rates on items that plainly cost money — the typed-zero receipt, the opening line that missed its rate.
2. Implausibly high rates — the drift eye's escapees.
3. Each line traced to the ledger row that set the rate (Chapter 2's voucher trace) and corrected through its door (Chapter 4).

3. The negative-stock damage read. Module 1 recommended Allow Negative Stock off; the valuation reason completes the case: an issue posted from a negative or zero balance prices at a rate the ledger cannot honestly know, and the eventual correcting receipt does not retroactively fix what the issues already posted to cost. Where negatives exist, the standing read lists them (module 1); each closed by its explaining document; and the switch goes off once the register is clean — permanently, because Chapter 8's case is what the switch left on becomes.

4. The margin sanity read — monthly, with the accountant. Gross margin by item group against expectation: a group whose margin moved with no price event has a cost side moving — a valuation drift surfacing in the one report managers actually watch. The read is the accountant's; the stock operator's part is the ledger investigation behind any flagged group (Chapter 2's item-story read, applied to the group's largest movers).

5. The opening-rate check — once, at every go-live and every new-branch load. Module 4's rule restated as a valuation read: opening rates sampled against recent purchase documents before the opening reconciliation submits. The classic error this catches is the opening stock loaded at selling price instead of cost — the error that overstates stock by the margin and understates every subsequent month's profit, and whose remediation months later is a ledger-level correction project (Chapter 8's second act). Ten sampled lines at go-live against a remediation project later: the lowest-cost read in the module.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the valuation year and the remediation
lessons.html:
This chapter runs Chapters 2-7 through HealthTrade's valuation year, including the inherited remediation. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the inherited state. The valuation review at the start of the year finds two inherited conditions from the pre-discipline era: Allow Negative Stock switched on — enabled in week two of the original go-live to silence posting errors, and left on for four years — with a tail of negative balances across the register; and a scatter of strange valuation rates from the same era.

Step 2 — the negative-stock remediation (Chapters 6-7). Run as a project with the accountant and the sysadmin per Chapter 6's rule 4: the negative balances listed and each closed by its explaining document (the unposted receipts entered on honest dates, the confirmed losses issued through the ladder); the correction batches entered in quiet windows with the repost queue watched to completion; the tie-out re-run after each batch. With the register clean, Allow Negative Stock goes off permanently — the setting change recorded with the remediation's file, and the weekly negative read retiring to a confirmation that stays empty.

Step 3 — the drift eye catches its case (Chapter 7). A receiving line enters at ₦96,000 against the item's ₦9,600 history. The line stops at the check: the trace finds a carton rate typed against a unit line — the UoM slip — corrected at the dock before submission. The counterfactual is stated in the month's note for the training file: uncaught, the rate would have inflated the average and mis-priced every subsequent issue until a margin review found it.

Step 4 — the container question answered from the ledger (Chapter 3). The owner asks whether this week's deliveries are consuming the cheap June container or March's dearer one. The answer runs from the item's ledger in five minutes: the item values under Moving Average; the Valuation Rate column shows the average stepping down at the June receipt row; deliveries since price at the blended figure. The margin improvement is shown as arithmetic on the ledger — the item-story read doing its standing job.

Step 5 — the landed-cost discipline lands (Chapter 4). The year's import consignments each carry a Landed Cost Voucher from the clearing file: charges allocated by the accountant's per-cost-type basis, entered when the costs are known, the repost queue watched on the two vouchers that landed onto prior-week receipts. The margin by item group steadies as import costs stop leaking into period expenses.

Step 6 — the year's rhythm. The monthly tie-out runs twelve times: eleven zeros; one difference traced in twenty minutes to a manual journal a new accounts officer posted to the stock account — reversed, re-expressed through the proper document, and the account's manual-posting restriction confirmed with the sysadmin. The weekly strange-rate read stays short after quarter one. The year closes with the valuation page to the MD: the tie-out record, the remediation file closed, the drift-eye catches logged, and the stock figure handed to the year-end close reconciled to the ledger it stands on.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in valuation, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the typed strange rate. Symptom: a receipt rate an order of magnitude off history; the average polluted; issues mis-priced until a review notices. Correction: the voucher corrected through its door; the repost recomputing downstream. Prevention: the last-paid drift eye at entry with the deviation warning treated as a stop.

Error 2 — freight expensed, stock undervalued. Symptom: import costs sitting in period expenses; stock carried at bare invoice price; margins mis-timed. Correction: Landed Cost Vouchers entered for the affected receipts with the queue watched. Prevention: the consignment rule — the voucher when costs are known, on every import the policy names.

Error 3 — the manual journal to stock. Symptom: the tie-out breaking by a round figure; a general-ledger entry with no stock ledger behind it. Correction: the journal reversed and re-expressed through the stock-side document. Prevention: nobody journals the stock accounts by hand, and the account-level posting restriction enforcing it.

Error 4 — negatives left on. Symptom: issues priced from balances the ledger cannot know; corrections that never retroactively fix posted cost; the switch left on for years to silence errors it was hiding. Correction: the remediation project — negatives closed by document, the switch off permanently. Prevention: the switch off from day one and the register's discipline making it unnecessary.

Error 5 — opening stock at selling price. Symptom: stock overstated by the margin from day one; profit understated monthly; the eventual correction a ledger-level project. Correction: the remediation with the accountant — the professional correction of the opening rates and their downstream effects. Prevention: the opening-rate sample against purchase documents before the opening reconciliation submits.

Error 6 — changes stacked onto reposts. Symptom: corrections entered while large reposts run; the queue compounding; the tie-out read mid-flight and mistrusted. Correction: the queue drained, the tie-out re-run clean. Prevention: Chapter 6's operating rules — large corrections scheduled, the queue watched to completion, the tie-out after.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: read a Stock Ledger Entry column by column and narrate one item's story; compute both methods on paper and answer the container question under each; name the four doors rates enter through and the one door that does not exist; walk the Landed Cost Voucher with its distribution bases; state what each document posts and run the monthly tie-out with its cause list; operate the repost rules including the failed-job incident and the remediation-as-project discipline; and run the five rate-error reads on their cadences.

Module rule 5: value follows the documents — rates born at their four doors and nowhere else, landed costs on every named consignment, methods set by recorded policy, the stock ledger tied to the accounts at zero every month, backdating carrying its repost cost consciously, and every strange rate stopped at entry. Module 6 covers the branch network.

branch_network.title: Inventory 6 — The Branch Network
branch_network.desc: The branch network in ZhiftERP: the hub-and-spoke replenishment model and the purchasing boundary; Material Requests with purpose Material Transfer and the item reorder table reasoning on projected quantities; the weekly replenishment run — inputs, the review pass with reasoned adjustments, the despatch pass through transit, and the closing note; allocation under scarcity by written rule — the essential floor first, pro-rata by sell-through, documented and communicated, with the relief despatch and the pattern check; opening a new branch by transfer with the ninety-day weekly review cycle and day-sixty reorder levels; laterals, returns, and the exception purchase lane; and the six branch reads on their cadences.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The branch network: scope and model
lessons.html:
This module covers multi-site stock operations in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: operate the hub-and-spoke replenishment model with Material Requests and reorder levels; run the weekly replenishment cycle; allocate stock under scarcity by written rule; open a new branch's stock by transfer with the tight first cycle; run laterals and enforce the purchasing boundary; and read the branch network's standing reports.

The model, stated once. Modules 1-5 built the machinery: warehouses with custody, transfers through transit, identity on movements, counts proving custody, value following documents. This module is that machinery operating as a network. The standing design from module 1's worked example:

1. Central buys. Procurement concentrates at the hub — supplier terms, receiving discipline, landed costs, and the quality gate all live once, at Central.
2. Branches sell and request. A branch's stock arrives by transfer from Central; the branch's job is selling, counting, and requesting — not supplier management.
3. Everything moves by the modules already built: requests as documents, despatches through transit (module 2), identity travelling (module 3), receipts counted against despatches, value carried by the ledger (module 5).

Why the boundary matters. The branch that buys locally outside the lanes acquires stock at unmatched prices with no receiving control, no landed costs, no batch capture, and no supplier accountability — five modules of discipline bypassed in one purchase. Chapter 6 covers the exception lane for the genuine emergency; the boundary itself is policy, written in module 1 and enforced here.

Custody at network scale. Each site's keeper answers for their warehouses (module 1); the stock manager at Central owns the network flows — the replenishment run, the allocation decisions, the lateral approvals; the reads (Chapter 7) are how the center maintains oversight of stock at remote sites. The division is the programme's standing shape: the sites execute and attest locally, the center decides and reads network-wide, and every flow between them is a document.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the request machinery — Material Requests and reorder levels. Chapter 3: the weekly replenishment run. Chapter 4: allocation under scarcity. Chapter 5: opening a new branch. Chapter 6: laterals, returns, and the purchasing boundary. Chapter 7: the branch reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The request machinery
lessons.html:
Branch demand reaches Central as documents. Two instruments: the Material Request, and the reorder levels that raise requests automatically.

1. The Material Request. Open Material Request (awesome bar) > New:

1. Purpose: Material Transfer — the branch's ask for stock from another warehouse (the purchase-purpose requests belong to the Procurement track; the transfer purpose is this module's instrument).
2. The rows — item, quantity, the requesting warehouse (Set From/Target per the form: the branch's stock room as the destination), and the required-by date.
3. Submission — the request becomes a visible, countable demand: the replenishment run works from submitted requests, the Ordered/Requested figures feed projected quantities (module 1, Chapter 6), and the request's fulfilment status tracks what the despatches delivered against it.

2. Reorder levels — the automatic ask. On the Item record, the reorder table carries one row per warehouse:

1. Warehouse — the branch stock room the rule watches.
2. Re-order Level — the projected-quantity threshold: when the warehouse's projected quantity falls below it, the system raises a Material Request automatically.
3. Re-order Qty — the quantity the raised request asks for.
4. Material Request Type: Transfer — the branch rows request transfer from the hub; purchase-type rows belong at Central where buying happens.

3. Setting the levels. The arithmetic is written, per item per branch, from the sell-through data (Chapter 7): the level covers expected sales across the replenishment interval plus the transit lead time, with the buffer the policy sets per item class (essential lines carry larger buffers; module 7's classifications feed this). The levels are reviewed quarterly against actual sell-through — a level set once and never revisited drifts into stockouts on rising lines and overstock on falling ones, which is exactly the pattern the quarterly review reads for.

4. The request disciplines.

1. Projected, not actual: the trigger and the manual request alike reason on projected quantity — stock on the shelf minus commitments plus what is already coming. A branch that requests on shelf-count alone double-orders what is already in transit to it.
2. Requests are honest asks: the branch requests what the data supports, not a padded figure hedging against short allocation — Chapter 4's allocation rules exist precisely so padding is unnecessary, and the run compares requests against sell-through (Chapter 3) so padding is also visible.
3. One request per branch per cycle as the standing rhythm (plus the exception request for the genuine urgent case, flagged as such): the run works a predictable queue, and the branch consolidates its week's needs into one reviewable document.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The weekly replenishment run
lessons.html:
The replenishment cycle runs weekly. This chapter is the procedure, step by step, as the stock manager runs it.

1. The inputs, assembled (thirty minutes).

1. The submitted Material Requests — the branches' consolidated asks plus any auto-raised reorder requests since last run.
2. The sell-through view (Chapter 7) — each branch's recent movement on the requested lines.
3. The hub's availability — Central's projected quantities on the requested items.
4. The transit state — module 2's read: what is already moving, so the run does not re-send what is on the road.

2. The review pass. Per request line: the ask against the branch's sell-through and current projected quantity. Three outcomes:

1. Approved as asked — the data supports it.
2. Adjusted with a note — the ask disagrees with the data (the padded line, the forgotten in-transit quantity); adjusted quantities carry one-line reasons back to the branch, so the branch can correct its next request from the same data.
3. Held for the scarcity procedure — total asks exceed hub availability on a line: Chapter 4 takes over for that line.

3. The despatch pass. The approved quantities become the pick list per branch; module 2's machinery executes:

1. One despatch entry per vehicle-load per branch (Add to Transit), submitted as the truck loads, batches on the rows (module 3).
2. The despatch references the Material Requests it fulfils — the request's status tracks fulfilment, and the branch sees what is coming against what it asked.
3. The branch receives against the despatch rows — identity and quantity confirmed, shortfalls per module 2's procedure.

4. The run's closing note. Ten lines, filed weekly: requests received and their total lines, adjustments made with reasons, scarcity lines and their allocations (Chapter 4), despatches submitted with references, and the exceptions carried to next run. The note is the run's audit trail and the new stock manager's training file — the run must be a procedure a competent person can take over from the file, per the programme's handover standard.

5. The cadence decision. Weekly is the standing default; the policy sets it per the business's rhythm. The rule that governs any cadence: the replenishment interval plus transit lead time is the window the reorder arithmetic covers (Chapter 2) — shortening the cycle without recomputing levels overstocks the branches; lengthening it without recomputing understocks them. Cycle and levels move together or not at all.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Allocation under scarcity
lessons.html:
When the hub cannot fill every approved ask, allocation becomes a decision. The rule of this chapter: scarcity is allocated by written rule, documented, and communicated.

1. When the procedure triggers. The run's review pass (Chapter 3) finds a line where the branches' approved asks total more than Central's available quantity — the supplier short-shipped, demand spiked, or an import is late. The line moves from the despatch pass into this procedure.

2. The written allocation rules. The policy page, agreed with the owner before the first scarce week, in application order:

1. The essential floor first. For items the policy marks essential (the classification from module 7's data plus the business's judgment — for a pharmaceutical network, the critical-care lines), every stocking branch receives the floor quantity before anything else allocates. The floor is a written per-item figure, sized to the minimum service level the business will not breach at any branch.
2. Pro-rata by sell-through above the floor. The remaining quantity divides across branches in proportion to their recent sell-through on the line (Chapter 7's eight-week read) — the stock goes where it is provably selling, by arithmetic anyone can check.
3. Rounding to shippable units — cartons round per the policy's rule, differences carried to next cycle rather than argued.

3. The documentation. The allocation worksheet files with the run's note: the line, the available quantity, each branch's ask and sell-through figure, the floor applied, the pro-rata arithmetic, and the allocated result. The worksheet is the answer to every version of the question one branch will ask — why did the other site get more — and the answer is the recorded calculation.

4. The communication. Each affected branch receives, with its despatch advice: the allocated quantity against its ask, the one-line reason (short supply; floor plus pro-rata applied), and the expected relief date if known (the purchase order's schedule from the Procurement track). Branches that understand the rule stop padding requests (Chapter 2's discipline holding), because padding cannot move a pro-rata allocation built on sell-through data — the arithmetic ignores the ask's size beyond eligibility.

5. The scarcity aftermath. Two follow-ups close the loop:

1. The relief despatch — when supply lands, the shorted branches are made whole first, from the worksheet's carried differences, before the normal cycle resumes.
2. The pattern check — a line hitting the scarcity procedure repeatedly is a purchasing signal, not an allocation problem: the reorder arithmetic at the hub (Central's own levels against total network demand) goes to the procurement owner with the worksheets as data.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Opening a new branch
lessons.html:
A new branch's stock is a project with a checklist. This chapter is the procedure, and its two governing rules: the branch opens by transfer, never by reconciliation, and opening estimates differ from actual demand — so the first ninety days run on a weekly review cycle.

1. The structural prerequisites (module 1's work). Before any stock moves: the site's warehouses created in the tree per the convention (the stock room, and the specials the site needs); the keeper and deputy named on the custody list; user permissions scoping the branch team; the POS profile's warehouse pointing at the branch stock room (the ZhiftPOS track's commissioning); the Item Defaults reviewed for the site where the wiring convention requires it.

2. The opening range and quantities. The range list builds from the nearest comparable branch's data — its stocking list and sell-through, adjusted for the new site's expected profile. The plan states the standing assumption: these figures are estimates, they will differ from actual demand item by item, and the correction mechanism is the first-cycle review (step 4), not revision of the estimates.

3. The opening transfer. The opening stock despatches from Central as ordinary two-step transfers (module 2): despatch entries with batches on the rows, transit legs, the branch receiving against despatch rows with full counting discipline. Why never a reconciliation: an opening reconciliation types quantities and rates into existence with no document trail behind them (module 5's opening-rate hazards, recreated voluntarily at every branch), while a transfer moves documented, valued, identified stock — the bins open true, the batches arrive with their expiries, the values carry from the ledger, and day one's records are as trustworthy as Central's. The reconciliation instrument is not used at branch openings; the Opening Stock purpose belongs to the company's original implementation, not to branch expansion.

4. The first ninety days — the weekly review cycle. Because the opening estimates will differ from actual demand:

1. Weekly sell-through review, line by line — the new branch's movement against the opening assumptions, read every week for the first ninety days (against the standing network's routine cadence).
2. Replenishment on the data, not the plan — the weekly run treats the new branch's requests with fresh eyes: the fast movers identified and levels set from actual sales; the dead openers flagged early for lateral return (Chapter 6) before they age into module 7's problem lists.
3. Reorder levels written at day sixty — enough data to set the Chapter 2 arithmetic honestly; the automatic machinery takes over from manual review as the levels prove out.
4. The first cycle count inside month one — module 4's programme starts immediately at the new site; the first month's count closes the branch's bins against physical truth while every discrepancy is young and traceable.

5. The opening file. The checklist, the range list with its source data, the opening despatch references, the weekly review notes, and the day-sixty level decisions — one folder, the branch's stock history from its first carton, per the standing one-lookup standard.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Laterals, returns, and the purchasing boundary
lessons.html:
Three flows complete the network's movement set: branch-to-branch laterals, returns to the hub, and the exception lane at the purchasing boundary.

1. Laterals — branch to branch. The case: one branch overstocks what another sells (the rebalancing read, Chapter 7, or a scarcity relief). The rules:

1. Approved at the center — laterals are proposed by the read or the branches but approved by the stock manager, because the network view (what is in transit, what the run is about to despatch) lives at Central and a well-meant lateral can cross a replenishment already moving.
2. Executed as standard transfers — two-step through transit where sites are apart (module 2), identity on the rows (module 3), received against despatch. A lateral is a standard transfer with every control applied.
3. Recorded with its reason — the lateral's note names the read or decision behind it; the quarterly lateral census (Chapter 7) reads the pattern, because recurring laterals on a line mean the allocation or the levels are wrong at the source.

2. Returns to the hub. Slow stock, near-expiry lines moving to where they sell (module 3's rebalancing lane), range delistings, and recalled goods all flow branch-to-Central as transfers with their reasons. The receiving discipline holds in reverse: Central counts the return against the despatch, and near-expiry returns land per module 3's lanes rather than disappearing into the main store.

3. The purchasing boundary and its exception lane. The policy from module 1: branches do not buy. The exception lane, for the genuine case (the emergency purchase the service level requires and Central cannot despatch in time):

1. Pre-approved in writing — the branch requests, the stock manager or owner approves per the threshold, before the purchase.
2. Executed through the purchasing documents — the Procurement track's flow at branch scale: a real order, a real receipt at the branch's warehouse, the invoice matched. The exception uses the lanes at small scale; it never bypasses them.
3. Listed monthly — every exception purchase on one list to the owner with reasons. The list's healthy state is nearly empty; a branch appearing repeatedly is a replenishment failure to fix at the run (the levels, the cadence, the transit time); recurring exceptions indicate the boundary is no longer being enforced.

4. What never happens, restated. Stock does not move between branches on a phone call; purchases do not happen on a branch manager's card with the paperwork to follow; returns do not accumulate in a back room awaiting a quiet month. Every flow in this chapter uses the standard documents with a recorded reason.
