lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The branch reads
lessons.html:
These reads give the center its oversight of stock at remote sites. Each is stated with its cadence, its source, and its action.

1. The sell-through read — weekly, per branch. The eight-week movement view per item per branch (the sales and issue history from the ledger, compiled by the standing report): what each branch actually sells, trended. This read is the module's most frequently used figure — it feeds the replenishment review (Chapter 3), the allocation arithmetic (Chapter 4), the new-branch cycle (Chapter 5), and the rebalancing proposals below. The sell-through percentage per line (units sold against units stocked across the window) is the comparable figure: a line at 58% at Ibadan and 12% at Akure is a rebalancing candidate readable in one row.

2. The branch stock page — monthly, to the owner. One page per branch with the close: stock value (the Stock Balance at the site's group node, using module 1's tree structure), the value trend, the site's count accuracy (module 4's metric per warehouse), open transit lines, and the month's exceptions (shortfalls, exception purchases, laterals). The page is the branch's stock health in five figures, comparable across sites and months.

3. The rebalancing read — monthly. The sell-through comparison across branches on common lines: overstocked-here-selling-there candidates, proposed as laterals with the arithmetic attached (Chapter 6's approval lane). The read proposes; the stock manager disposes — and the standing preference order is levels-fix first, lateral second: a lateral corrects a symptom once, the level correction stops it recurring.

4. The network accuracy comparison — monthly. Module 4's accuracy metric side by side across sites. The trailing site gets the next spot count and the process review as data — the same read the counting module defined, operated at network scale.

5. The transit and boundary reads — weekly. Module 2's transit age read run network-wide (every aged line named to its despatch), and the monthly exception-purchase list (Chapter 6). Both are boundary-integrity reads: the network's rules hold exactly as well as these lists stay short.

6. The reorder health read — quarterly. Chapter 2's levels against the quarter's actual sell-through, per branch: lines whose levels triggered stockouts (level too low or transit slower than assumed), lines that never triggered while stock aged (level too high or line dying — module 7's territory adjoins here). The read closes with level corrections written and dated, which is what keeps the automatic machinery calibrated to the business the branches actually do.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade opens Akure, and the Emzor short-close
lessons.html:
This chapter runs Chapters 2-7 through two network events. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Event 1 — opening Akure (Chapter 5).

1. Prerequisites: the Akure warehouses stand in the tree from module 1's design; the keeper and deputy named; permissions scoped; the POS profile pointed at Akure - Stock Room.
2. The range: built from Ibadan's stocking list and sell-through as the comparable, trimmed for the smaller catchment — with the plan stating the standing assumption: these are estimates and the first-cycle review will correct them.
3. The opening transfer: despatched from Central as standard two-step transfers, batches on every row, received at Akure against despatch rows. Opening by transfer, never reconciliation — Akure's bins open documented, valued, and identified from the first carton.
4. The weekly review cycle: line-by-line sell-through review for ninety days. Week three shows the first differences from the estimates: four lines selling at twice the estimate, and a tail of slow openers flagged early. Replenishment follows the data; two dead openers return to Central by lateral in week six before aging into a problem list; reorder levels write at day sixty from actual sales. The first cycle count runs inside month one and month one closes with Akure's bins true — the opening file holding the checklist, despatch references, weekly notes, and level decisions.

Event 2 — the Emzor short-close (Chapter 4). A supplier short-ships a fast Emzor line into a demand spike: the weekly run finds branch asks totalling 300 cartons against 180 available across the three sites. The line moves to the allocation procedure:

1. The essential floor first: the line is on the essential list; the written floor of 30 cartons per stocking branch allocates 90 across the three sites before anything else.
2. Pro-rata by sell-through: the remaining 90 divide in proportion to each branch's eight-week sell-through on the line — the arithmetic on the worksheet, checkable by anyone.
3. Documented and communicated: the worksheet files with the run's note; each branch receives its allocation with the one-line reason and the relief date from the purchase order's schedule. The question one branch manager asks — why did Ibadan get more — is answered by the worksheet's sell-through column in one look.
4. The aftermath: the relief despatch makes the shorted branches whole first when supply lands the following week; the pattern check finds this the line's first scarcity event in the year — no purchasing signal, the worksheet files, the cycle resumes.

The month's network page. The branch pages to the MD show: Akure's opening month with bins true and its first accuracy figure; Ibadan's 58% sell-through on the watched line against Akure's early figures feeding the rebalancing read; transit at zero aged lines through both events; the exception-purchase list empty — the boundary held through the scarce month.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in network operations, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — requests from the shelf, not the projection. Symptom: branches double-ordering what is already in transit; overstock arriving in waves. Correction: the affected lines rebalanced; the request discipline re-briefed. Prevention: requests and reorder triggers reasoning on projected quantity — shelf minus commitments plus incoming.

Error 2 — the padded ask. Symptom: requests inflated to hedge against short allocation; the run's data polluted; trust eroding both directions. Correction: adjustments with reasons; the allocation rules communicated. Prevention: Chapter 4's arithmetic — pro-rata on sell-through ignores the size of the ask, so padding does not change the allocation and is visible in the review.

Error 3 — the branch opened by reconciliation. Symptom: opening quantities and rates typed into existence; no document trail; module 5's opening hazards recreated at branch scale. Correction: where recent, the reconciliation reversed and the opening re-run by transfer; where aged, the valuation review with the accountant. Prevention: the rule — branches open by transfer, and the Opening Stock purpose belongs to the original implementation only.

Error 4 — estimates defended instead of corrected. Symptom: the new branch replenished to the plan for months; fast lines stocked out while dead openers age. Correction: the weekly review cycle started late — weekly reads, levels from actuals. Prevention: the standing assumption written into the opening plan: estimates differ from actual demand, and the first ninety days are reviewed weekly.

Error 5 — the informal lateral. Symptom: stock moving between branches on phone calls; transfers crossing replenishments already in transit; the center's network view wrong. Correction: the movements documented; the approval lane restored. Prevention: laterals approved at Central and executed as standard transfers with recorded reasons.

Error 6 — the exception that became a habit. Symptom: one branch's emergency purchases recurring monthly; the boundary no longer enforced. Correction: the replenishment failure fixed at its source — the levels, the cadence, or the transit assumption. Prevention: the monthly exception list to the owner, reviewed for replenishment failures at their source.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the hub-and-spoke model and why the purchasing boundary exists; raise and review Material Requests and set reorder rows with the projected-quantity arithmetic; run the weekly cycle — inputs, review pass with reasoned adjustments, despatch pass, closing note; allocate scarcity by the written rules — floor first, pro-rata by sell-through, documented and communicated, with the relief and pattern follow-ups; open a branch by transfer with the ninety-day weekly review cycle and day-sixty levels; operate laterals, returns, and the exception lane; and run the six branch reads on their cadences.

Module rule 6: the network replenishes by procedure — requests reasoned on projected quantities, a weekly run with reasoned adjustments, scarcity allocated by written rule and shown as arithmetic, branches opened by transfer and reviewed weekly for ninety days, and every flow through the standard machinery with a reason attached. Module 7 covers stock health and analytics.

stock_health.title: Inventory 7 — Stock Health & Analytics
stock_health.desc: Stock health and analytics in ZhiftERP: the stock aging read with its bands, the over-ninety-day percentage, and the carried working list; movement classification and the two-dimensional grid with seasonal and probation exclusions; sell-through analytics — the network view, the divergence read, the group rollup, and the like-window rule; the five dead-stock lanes in preference order with the monthly review's decision list; upstream prevention — reorder hygiene, purchasing feedback, the range review and delisting execution, and the new-item probation read; and stock turns, the joined margin reading, and the five-section monthly health page.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Stock health: scope and reads
lessons.html:
This module covers stock health and analytics in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: run the stock aging read and maintain the over-ninety-day working list; classify items by movement and combine the classification with value ranking; run sell-through analytics at network and site level; operate the dead-stock lanes in their preference order with their documents; apply the upstream prevention reads; compute stock turns and compile the monthly health page.

What stock health means. Modules 1-6 keep the records accurate. This module reads those records to answer a different question: is the stock itself in good condition as an investment? Stock that does not move ties up money, occupies space, approaches expiry, and eventually writes off. The reads in this module identify that stock early, while the corrective lanes still have options; the lanes then move, reprice, return, or write off the identified stock by document.

The read-and-lane structure. Each read produces a list; each list feeds a lane; each lane is a documented procedure with an owner and an approval level. The reads are scheduled, not occasional: a stock health problem identified at month three costs a markdown; the same problem identified at month eleven costs a write-off.

Custody. The stock manager runs the reads and prepares the lists; the owner decides the lanes at the monthly review for items above the threshold; the stock function executes the decided lanes through the standard documents (modules 2, 3, and 6). Purchasing receives the upstream findings (Chapter 6), because most stock health problems are purchasing decisions read back three months later.

The data precondition. Every read in this module computes from the ledger and the movement history. The reads are reliable to the degree modules 1-5 are operated: accurate quantities (module 4's counts), honest dates (module 2's posting discipline), correct values (module 5). A site with weak record discipline reads its stock health from fiction; the accuracy metric (module 4) is therefore the first figure on the health page, because it states how much the other figures can be trusted.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the stock aging read. Chapter 3: movement classification. Chapter 4: sell-through analytics. Chapter 5: the dead-stock lanes. Chapter 6: upstream prevention. Chapter 7: turns, margin, and the health page. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

Why this module is read monthly rather than annually. Every figure in it moves slowly and compounds — stock ages a month at a time, a slowing item slows quietly, and a reorder level set for last year's demand keeps ordering until somebody looks. Read annually, all of it arrives at once as a large uncomfortable number nobody can act on. Read monthly, each finding is small enough to have a lane and an owner, which is the difference between a health review and a write-off.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The stock aging read
lessons.html:
The aging read groups stock value by how long it has been held. This chapter is the report, the bands, and the working list.

1. The Stock Ageing report. Open Stock Ageing (awesome bar) — the standing report over the ledger's receipt history. Per item per warehouse it computes the age of the held stock from the receipt dates of the quantities still on hand (the earliest-in quantities age first, consistent with the receipt-queue arithmetic), and presents the age columns with quantities and values.

2. The band structure. The policy sets the bands; the standing shape for a trading business: 0-30 days, 31-60, 61-90, and over 90. For a pharmaceutical distributor the bands read alongside module 3's expiry horizons — age and remaining shelf life are different measures (a slow item bought with long dating ages without expiry risk; a fast item bought short-dated expires without aging), and the two reads are run separately for that reason.

3. The monthly compile. With the close, per warehouse and for the network:

1. The value per band — the aging profile: how much of the stock investment sits in each band.
2. The over-ninety-day line as a percentage of total stock value — the single-figure trend. The percentage is the comparable number across months and sites; the policy sets the target and the review threshold.
3. The over-ninety-day working list — every item in the band with quantity, value, warehouse, and last movement date. This list is the module's primary working document: Chapter 5's lanes work through it item by item at the monthly review.

4. Reading the profile. Three standing observations the compile is checked for:

1. A growing over-ninety band — stock entering the band faster than the lanes clear it: either the lanes are not running or purchasing is over-buying (Chapter 6's feedback loop).
2. Band concentration by item group — one group carrying a disproportionate share of the aged value directs the review to a range or supplier decision rather than item-by-item treatment.
3. Band concentration by site — aged stock concentrated at one branch feeds module 6's rebalancing read before any markdown is considered: stock aged at one site may sell at its normal price at another.

5. The read's discipline. The working list carries forward month to month with each item's lane decision and status. An item appearing on the list for a second month without a decision is an escalation to the owner per the review procedure — the list exists to force decisions, and an undecided item is the list failing at its purpose.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Movement classification
lessons.html:
Value ranking (module 4's ABC) and movement speed are different measurements. This chapter combines them into the two-dimensional read that sets priorities.

1. The movement classes. Per item per site, computed from consumption over the policy's window (the standing window: two quarters):

1. Fast — consistent movement across the window at or above the group's median.
2. Slow — movement present but below the median, or irregular across the window.
3. Dead — negligible or zero movement across the window. The policy defines negligible numerically (for example, fewer than a set number of units across the window), so the classification is computed, not judged.

2. Why value ranking alone is insufficient. Module 4's ABC classification ranks by consumption value and directs counting effort. A C-class item — low individual value — can be dead in large numbers: individually each line is small, and collectively the class ties up significant value and shelf space while attracting no attention precisely because each line is small. The movement classification exists to read what value ranking passes over.

3. The two-dimensional read. The classes cross into a priority grid, worked in this order at the review:

1. High-value dead (A or B class, dead movement) — the priority cell: significant money not moving. Each line is worked individually through Chapter 5's lanes at the first review it appears.
2. Low-value dead in volume (C class, dead movement) — worked as a set: the count of lines and their aggregate value are the review figures, and the treatment is usually collective — a range decision, a clearance programme, or the delisting flow (module 8) — rather than line-by-line handling.
3. High-value slow — the watch cell: reorder levels checked against the movement (Chapter 6) before more arrives.
4. Fast items — no health action; their reads belong to replenishment (module 6).

4. The classification cadence. Computed quarterly alongside the ABC review (module 4's cadence), stored per item per site, and compared against the prior quarter: items newly entering the dead class are the early-warning list — a line that was slow last quarter and dead this quarter is identified two quarters earlier than the aging read alone would surface it, because aging measures the stock already held while movement measures the demand that stopped.

5. The classification's limits, stated. Seasonal items classify as dead in their off season by construction; the classification read carries a seasonal flag per the range list, and flagged items are assessed against the same window of the prior year (Chapter 4's like-window rule) rather than the preceding quarter. New items inside their probation window (Chapter 6) are excluded from the dead class until the probation read completes.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Sell-through analytics
lessons.html:
Module 6 defined the eight-week sell-through read for replenishment. This chapter extends it into the analytical views the health reviews use.

1. The base figure, restated. Sell-through per item per site: units sold across the window as a percentage of units available across the window (opening stock plus receipts). The figure states demand against stocking, and it is comparable across items, sites, and periods — the property the views below depend on.

2. The network view. The same item's sell-through across all sites, side by side:

1. Uniform low — the item is not selling anywhere: a range or pricing question for the review, and a candidate for Chapter 5's lanes.
2. Divergent — selling at one site, standing at another: module 6's rebalancing case, proposed as a lateral with the figures attached. The divergence read runs before any markdown decision, because moving stock to where it sells at full price precedes discounting it where it does not.
3. Uniform high with stockouts — the replenishment question (module 6's reorder health read), not a health problem.

3. The group rollup. Sell-through aggregated by item group: the view that supports range decisions. A group whose sell-through declines across two consecutive windows while its stock value holds or grows is accumulating aged stock by arithmetic — the compile flags it before the aging read shows the result, and the finding routes to the range review (Chapter 6) with the purchasing data attached.

4. The like-window rule. Comparisons run against comparable periods: this eight-week window against the same window of the prior year for seasonal ranges, against the preceding window for stable ranges. The range list marks which items are seasonal (Chapter 3's flag); the compile applies the correct comparison per the flag. A seasonal item compared against its own peak reads as collapsing; compared against last year's same season it reads correctly, and the rule exists because the wrong comparison generates false entries on the review lists.

5. The compile discipline. The sell-through views compile monthly with the close, from the standard reports, by the documented procedure — the same figures every month, computed the same way, filed with the review pack. The reviews depend on trend, and trend depends on consistent computation: a figure computed differently between months produces movement that is method, not demand. Where the computation changes (a window resized, a group restructured), the change is recorded and the affected trend restarts from the change date.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The dead-stock lanes
lessons.html:
Identified dead stock is resolved through one of five lanes, in preference order, each by document. This chapter is the lanes and the monthly review that assigns them.

1. Lane 1 — rebalancing. The item sells at another site (Chapter 4's divergence read): a lateral transfer per module 6's procedure — proposed with the sell-through figures, approved at the center, executed as a standard transfer with identity on the rows. Rebalancing recovers full price and costs a transfer; it is first in preference for that reason.

2. Lane 2 — markdown. The item sells at a lower price: the markdown per the concession machinery (the ZhiftPOS track's markdown reasons and approval rules), with the dead-stock reason code, the price set per the policy's markdown ladder, and the review tracking sell-through at the new price. A markdown that does not move the stock within its review window escalates to the next lane rather than deepening indefinitely — the ladder's steps and windows are written in the policy.

3. Lane 3 — return to vendor. Supplier terms permit returns on the line: the Procurement track's return flow, initiated within the terms' window, batches named on the return, credit tracked to settlement. This lane's availability is a purchasing term decided at supplier onboarding; the health review's recurring use of it on one supplier's lines is feedback for the next negotiation (Chapter 6).

4. Lane 4 — bundling and substitution. The item moves as part of an offer or as a recommended substitute per the selling policy: the bundle or promotion machinery (the ZhiftPOS track's promotion configuration), with the dead-stock lines named in the offer's file. The lane applies where the item supports another sale even though it does not sell alone.

5. Lane 5 — write-off. The remaining case: no site sells it, no price moves it, no return applies, no offer carries it. The write-off posts through module 2's issue lane — the reason, the account, the evidence (the review's decision note), the approval per the value ladder — and the disposal follows the compliance rules where the goods are regulated. The write-off is a decided expense: it appears on the review's decision list, the owner approves it per the band, and the month's issues read (module 2) reports it with the other decided figures.

6. The monthly dead-stock review. The standing meeting, with the close: the over-ninety working list (Chapter 2) and the dead classification (Chapter 3) consolidated; each item or set assigned its lane with a one-line reason; prior months' assignments checked for status (the markdown that moved, the return awaiting credit, the lateral completed); undecided second-month items escalated per Chapter 2's rule. The review's output is the decision list — item, value, lane, owner, date — filed with the health page, and every decision on it is executable through a standard document the same week.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Upstream prevention
lessons.html:
The lanes resolve dead stock; this chapter reduces how much is created. Four upstream reads, each routing findings to the function that acts on them.

1. Reorder level hygiene. Module 6's quarterly reorder health read, applied with the health data: levels on items whose movement class fell (Chapter 3's early-warning list) are corrected the same quarter — a level set for a fast item continues ordering fast-item quantities into a slowing demand until someone corrects it, and the correction is the lowest-cost prevention in the module. The read closes with the corrections written and dated.

2. Purchasing feedback. Two standing figures route to the procurement owner monthly:

1. The aging profile by supplier — aged stock grouped by the supplier it was bought from: a supplier whose lines recur in the over-ninety band is a buying-quantity or line-selection question for the next purchasing review.
2. The expiry horizon profile (module 3's quarterly read) — the short-dated band's trend as purchasing feedback: buying outrunning sell-through shows here first for dated goods.

Both route as data with items and figures attached, per the standing data-not-editorial rule; the purchasing decisions belong to the Procurement track's reviews.

3. The range review and delisting. Twice yearly, from the group rollups (Chapter 4) and the dead classification (Chapter 3): lines the business decides to stop stocking exit through the delisting flow — remaining stock resolved through the lanes, reorder rows removed, the item retired per module 8's item lifecycle procedure (disabled at zero, never deleted). A delisting decided but not executed leaves reorder machinery ordering a discontinued line; the review's decision list therefore carries execution status until each line closes.

4. The new-item probation read. Every newly ranged item carries a probation window (the policy's figure — the standing shape: one quarter): stocked at the opening estimate, read weekly against sell-through in its first window per module 6's new-branch discipline applied at item scale, and confirmed, adjusted, or exited at the probation review. The read exists because new items are estimates by definition, and an estimate reviewed at week twelve costs at most one quarter's mis-stocking; an estimate never reviewed becomes the aging read's finding a year later at the full cost.

5. The prevention summary on the health page. One line per read on the monthly page (Chapter 7): reorder corrections made, the supplier aging figure, delisting execution status, probation outcomes. The summary states whether prevention is operating; a health page that reports only the lanes is reporting the cost of prevention not running.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Turns, margin, and the health page
lessons.html:
The module's output figures, and the one page that carries them monthly.

1. Stock turns. The standing efficiency figure: cost of goods sold across the period divided by average stock value across the period, annualised per the policy's convention. Computed per item group and for the whole:

1. The group comparison — groups compared against their own history and against the policy's expectation per group (fast-moving retail groups turn faster than equipment ranges by nature; the expectation is set per group, not globally).
2. The trend — turns improving means stock working harder: the same sales carried on less investment. The figure summarises the whole module's effect in one number, and for this reason it leads the health page.
3. The computation source — cost of goods sold from the accounts (module 5's perpetual postings), average stock from the Stock Balance history; both figures from the standard reports by the documented method, per Chapter 4's compile discipline.

2. The margin read, joined. Module 5's monthly margin-by-group read joins the health view here: a group with declining turns and stable margin is over-stocked; a group with stable turns and declining margin has a cost or pricing movement (module 5's territory); a group declining on both is a range question for Chapter 6's review. The joined reading directs each finding to its own procedure — the health page presents the figures side by side for exactly this reading.

3. The monthly health page. One page, with the close, to the owner:

1. Record reliability — the count accuracy metric per site (module 4): the figure that states how much the rest of the page can be trusted.
2. Total stock value and turns — the investment and its efficiency, trended.
3. The aging profile — value per band and the over-ninety percentage, trended (Chapter 2).
4. The dead-stock position — the working list's total value, the month's lane decisions and completions, the write-off total against its approvals (Chapter 5).
5. The prevention summary — Chapter 6's one-liners.

4. The page's discipline. The same five sections every month, computed the same way, one page in length. The page is the owner's standing answer to the condition of the stock investment; its trends are the module's evidence that the reads and lanes are working; and its preparation is a documented procedure the stock manager's deputy can execute, per the programme's handover standard.

Presenting the health page to an owner. Lead with turns and the over-ninety figure, both against their own history rather than against a target — an owner who has never seen these numbers needs the trend before the level, because the level alone invites an argument about whether it is good. Then the decisions taken since the last page and their outcomes. A page that reports figures without decisions gets read twice and then filed.

And the number to watch across a year. Not turns, which move with sales, but the over-ninety band as a percentage of stock value. It is the cleanest single measure of whether the lanes are being worked, because it rises whenever a read is compiled and nothing is done about it — and it cannot be improved by anything except decisions actually taken.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade's stock health year
lessons.html:
This chapter runs Chapters 2-7 through HealthTrade's first stock health year. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the first aging compile (Chapter 2). The first monthly compile establishes the baseline: the over-ninety-day band holds ₦6.2m — 9.6% of total stock value — concentrated at Central, with the working list running to several pages. The figure and the list go to the first monthly review with the band profile.

Step 2 — the two-dimensional read (Chapter 3). The movement classification computes alongside: the priority cell (high-value dead) holds a short list worked individually; the volume cell holds 140 C-class SKUs with negligible movement across two quarters — individually small lines, collectively a material value and a shelf-space cost, invisible to the value-ranked reads. The set is worked collectively per the procedure: a clearance programme for the bulk, and the delisting flow proposed for the tail.

Step 3 — the lanes run (Chapters 4-5).

1. Rebalancing first: the divergence read finds aged Central stock selling normally at the branches — ₦1.1m of the aged Akure-range allocation moves by two laterals to the sites where the sell-through data shows demand, recovering full price for a transfer's cost.
2. Markdown second: the named clearance lines enter the markdown ladder with the dead-stock reason code; the review window tracks movement at each step.
3. Vendor returns: two suppliers' lines return within terms, batches named, credits tracked to settlement; one supplier's recurring appearance files as negotiation feedback.
4. The residual write-off: the lines no lane moved post through the issue lane at the year's third review — a decided figure with the review's note attached, approved per the band.

Step 4 — prevention engages (Chapter 6). Reorder corrections write for every early-warning line the quarter it appears; the supplier aging figure starts routing monthly; the range review executes the first delisting batch through the retirement flow with execution status tracked to zero; the probation read exits two new lines at week twelve at one quarter's cost each.

Step 5 — the year's trend (Chapter 7). The health page runs twelve months on the same five sections. Year end against baseline: the over-ninety percentage below its opening figure and trending down; turns per group improved on the retail ranges as the cleared value converts to working stock; the write-off total for the year on the page against its approvals — a decided expense with its documents, arrived at after the cheaper lanes ran first; and the accuracy metric above target at every site, stating the page's own reliability. The year's file — twelve pages, twelve decision lists, the lane documents — answers any question about any line's treatment in one lookup.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in stock health, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — reads without lanes. Symptom: aging reports compiled and filed; the over-ninety band growing month over month; no decisions attached. Correction: the monthly review instituted, the working list worked item by item. Prevention: the read-and-lane structure — every list feeds a lane, and second-month undecided items escalate.

Error 2 — markdown as the first response. Symptom: aged stock discounted at the site it aged at while other sites sell it at full price. Correction: the divergence read run first; laterals where the data supports them. Prevention: the lane preference order — rebalancing before markdown, in the written procedure.

Error 3 — the invisible C-class accumulation. Symptom: value-ranked reads showing no problem while hundreds of small dead lines accumulate. Correction: the two-dimensional read computed; the volume cell worked collectively. Prevention: the quarterly movement classification alongside the ABC review.

Error 4 — seasonal false positives. Symptom: off-season items entering the dead lists; lanes run against demand that returns; the review lists losing credibility. Correction: the seasonal flags applied; comparisons re-run like for like. Prevention: the like-window rule and the range list's seasonal marking.

Error 5 — lanes without upstream fixes. Symptom: the same items cleared and re-accumulating; purchasing unaware of the aging its orders create. Correction: the prevention reads instituted and routed. Prevention: reorder hygiene the same quarter, the supplier aging figure monthly, and the probation read on every new line.

Error 6 — the inconsistent compile. Symptom: health figures computed differently between months; trends showing method changes as demand changes; reviews arguing about the numbers instead of the stock. Correction: the computation documented; affected trends restarted from the change date. Prevention: the compile discipline — the same figures, the same method, filed with the pack.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: run the aging read with its bands, the over-ninety percentage, and the carried working list; compute the movement classes and the two-dimensional grid with the seasonal and probation exclusions; run the sell-through views — network, divergence, group rollup — under the like-window rule; operate the five lanes in preference order with their documents and the monthly review's decision list; apply the four prevention reads with their routings; and compute turns, join the margin read, and compile the five-section health page.

Module rule 7: stock health is read on schedule and resolved by lane — aging and movement compiled monthly by the documented method, every listed item assigned a lane with its document, rebalancing before markdown and write-off last, findings routed upstream to purchasing and the range review, and the whole reported on one page whose first figure is the accuracy of the records it stands on. Module 8 covers settings, roles, and structure.

advanced_inventory.title: Inventory 8 — Advanced Inventory: Settings, Roles & Structure
advanced_inventory.desc: Settings, roles, and structure in ZhiftERP inventory: the Stock Settings walk — negative stock off, the freeze controls, tolerances with named exception roles, and reorder automation only on data-set levels — with the annual owner review; the stock control register with its row format and quarterly confirmation; the item lifecycle — the creation gate with the duplicate check, change governance, and the four-step retirement flow; the consolidated role matrix, the quarterly recertification, and the monthly adjustments read; the filing map, retention, the retrieval test, and the handover files; multi-company structure with the inter-company document rule; and the track recap of the eight module rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Advanced inventory: scope and structure
lessons.html:
This module completes the Inventory track with the structural layer: the settings, the register of control decisions, the item lifecycle, the role design, the records, and the multi-company structure. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Stock Settings walk and operate its annual review; maintain the stock control register; run the item lifecycle from the creation gate to the retirement flow; operate the role matrix with the recertification and the adjustments read; apply the records and handover conventions; and configure multi-company stock structure correctly.

Why the structural layer is its own module. Modules 1-7 taught the operating procedures. Each of those procedures depends on decisions made once and held: which settings are on, who holds which powers, how items enter and leave the register, where the evidence files. When the structural layer is maintained, the procedures run the same way regardless of who is present; when it is not, the procedures degrade into individual habits. The module's standing test — Chapter 8's worked example — is whether the stock function operates correctly through an extended absence of its most experienced people.

The three instruments.

1. The Stock Settings page (Chapter 2) — the system-wide switches, each set by decision and reviewed annually.
2. The control register (Chapter 3) — the one-table record of every stock control decision: what is set, to what value, decided by whom, for what reason, reviewed when.
3. The lifecycle and access procedures (Chapters 4-5) — how items and permissions change: by gate, by governance, by recertification.

Custody. The stock manager maintains the register and runs the reads; the owner decides the settings and the powers at the annual review and at every change; the sysadmin executes permission changes per the Sysadmin track's procedures. Setting changes follow the standing change discipline: written first, decided by the named owner, applied in a maintenance window where the change affects posting behaviour, and recorded in the register with the date of application.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Stock Settings walk. Chapter 3: the control register. Chapter 4: the item lifecycle. Chapter 5: roles, access, and the adjustments read. Chapter 6: records and handover. Chapter 7: multi-company structure. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review, the module rule, and the track recap.

What happens where this layer is skipped. The procedures still run, for as long as the people who learned them stay. Then a keeper leaves, a setting is changed by somebody solving a different problem, an item is created around the gate because the gate was never written down — and within a year the operating discipline has quietly become folklore that some sites follow and others do not. The structural layer is what makes modules 1 to 7 outlive the implementation.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Stock Settings walk
lessons.html:
Open Stock Settings (awesome bar). Walk the fields in order. Each carries a recommended posture, and every departure from it is a register entry with a reason.

1. Item defaults.

1. Item Naming By — item code entry convention (manual codes per the written coding scheme, or a naming series). Decided once at implementation; changing it mid-register is a governed event.
2. Default Warehouse — the final fallback of module 1's resolution chain. Set to the main central store; the monthly fallback read (module 1, Chapter 5) treats anything landing here as a wiring gap.
3. Default Valuation Method — the method items inherit where their own field is unset (module 5, Chapter 3). Set per the accountant's policy; the item-level field carries the exceptions.

2. Stock transaction controls.

1. Allow Negative Stock — off. The recommended posture from modules 1 and 5: a posting that would drive a balance negative is refused, forcing the missing document to be entered instead. The register records the posture and the module 5 remediation that enforced it.
2. Over-delivery and over-receipt allowances — the percentage tolerances for deliveries and receipts exceeding their orders. Set low per the policy; the tolerance is a control decision because it defines how far a document can depart from its authorisation before the system refuses.
3. Role Allowed to Over-deliver/Receive — where exceptional tolerance is granted, the named role holds it, per the register.

3. The freeze controls.

1. Stock Frozen Up To (date) — postings dated on or before this date are blocked for ordinary roles. Advanced with each period close per the Accounts track's calendar, and set for count windows (module 4, Chapter 3).
2. Stock Frozen Up To (days) — the rolling variant: postings older than the set number of days are blocked, which enforces module 2's same-day discipline as a system rule rather than a briefing point.
3. Role Allowed to Edit Frozen Stock — the exception role for postings into frozen dates. Held narrowly per the matrix; every use carries its reason per module 2's backdating lane.

4. Batch, serial, and reorder controls. The system-level defaults that support module 3's identity settings and module 6's reorder machinery — including the automatic Material Request generation switch for reorder rows. Each is set to serve the written procedures, and the reorder automation in particular is enabled only after module 6's levels are set from data, because automation ordering on unset levels generates requests nobody reviewed.

5. The annual settings review. Once a year, the stock manager and the owner walk this page against the control register: each setting confirmed still correct, each departure re-justified or corrected, the review dated in the register. Settings drift when nobody reads them; the annual walk is the standing correction, and the review's output is the register's next revision.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The stock control register
lessons.html:
The control register is one table holding every stock control decision. This chapter is its structure and operation.

1. The row format. Per control: the control's name, its current value or posture, the owner who decided it, the reason in one line, the date decided, and the next review date. One row per control; the register lives with the stock function's documents and is version-kept — superseded rows retained with their dates, so any past posture is answerable.

2. The register's contents. The rows collect the decisions modules 1-7 made, in one place:

1. Structure: the warehouse tree convention and level rule (module 1); the special warehouses in use; the default wiring convention.
2. Movement: the named Stock Entry Types; the issue and receipt lawful-case tables with the approval ladder; the backdating posture and its role; the transfer hygiene rules.
3. Identity: the item-class control table — batch posture, expiry, serials per class (module 3, Chapter 2); the recall procedure's owner and drill calendar.
4. Counting: the count cadences per warehouse; the threshold ladder's bands; the ABC review dates; the accuracy target.
5. Valuation: the method policy per class; the landed-cost consignment rule; the tie-out procedure; the revaluation lane's owner.
6. Network: the replenishment cadence; the allocation rules with the essential floor list; the branch purchasing boundary and its exception threshold; the lateral approval rule.
7. Health: the aging bands and the over-ninety target; the markdown ladder; the probation window; the review calendar.
8. Settings: every Chapter 2 posture with its reason.

3. Why one table. Distributed decisions are unauditable: the answer to how the stock function is controlled should not require reading seven procedures. The register is the one-lookup answer — for the owner's annual review, the external auditor's walkthrough, the new stock manager's first week, and the absence test (Chapter 8). It also exposes contradictions: two procedures carrying different thresholds for the same decision are visible only when both sit in one table.

4. The register's maintenance. Every control change lands in the register the day it is decided — the change is not complete until its row is updated. The quarterly review confirms the register against the live system (the settings page, the role matrix, the procedure documents); differences are corrected in whichever direction the owner's decision requires. A register that trails the system is a record of what used to be true, which for control purposes is the same as no register.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The item lifecycle
lessons.html:
Items enter the register by gate, change by governance, and leave by the retirement flow. This chapter is the three procedures.

1. The creation gate. New items are created against the checklist, by the roles the matrix permits:

1. The duplicate check first — the register searched by name fragments, barcode, and supplier reference before creation. A duplicate item splits one product's history across two records: stock in two places, reorder arithmetic on half the data, and counts that disagree by construction. The gate's search takes one minute; the merge remediation later takes days.
2. The class row applied — module 3's control table: the identity flags per the item's class, set at creation because retro-fitting over existing stock is a remediation.
3. The defaults wired — module 1's Item Defaults row per the convention; the UoM and conversion table per module 2's register where the item converts.
4. The commercial fields per their tracks — item group, prices, tax template (the Selling and Accounts tracks' territory), completed per the checklist so the item is fully operable at first receipt.
5. The probation flag — module 7's new-item window starts at creation.

2. Change governance. Item changes that affect posting behaviour — the valuation method, the identity flags, the UoM structure, the item group where accounts derive from it — are governed events per the standing change discipline: decided by the named owner, dated, and recorded. Descriptive changes (names, descriptions, images) are ordinary edits. The distinction is written in the procedure so the difference is a rule, not a judgment call per edit.

3. The retirement flow. Items leave the register by procedure, never by deletion:

1. The delisting decision — from the range review (module 7, Chapter 6), recorded with its reason.
2. Stock resolved through the lanes — the remaining balance cleared per module 7's preference order; the flow does not complete while stock remains.
3. The machinery disconnected — reorder rows removed at every site; the item taken off active price lists and offers per the selling procedures.
4. Disabled at zero — the item's Disabled flag set once every warehouse's balance is zero. The record remains readable forever: ledger history, past documents, and reports all reference it, and for this reason deletion is never the instrument.
5. The execution status tracked — module 7's rule: each delisting on the review's list until all four steps close.

4. The lifecycle reads. Monthly: items created in the month against the checklist (sampled); the duplicate-candidate report where the site runs one (near-identical names flagged for review). Quarterly: disabled items with non-zero balances (a retirement flow that skipped its steps — corrected through the lanes); active items with no movement and no probation flag feeding module 7's classification.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Roles, access, and the adjustments read
lessons.html:
The stock role design was built across modules 1-7. This chapter consolidates it and adds the standing reads that keep it true.

1. The matrix, consolidated. The stock section of the site's permission matrix, one row per power:

1. Stock User — daily movement documents within site scope (module 1's user permissions).
2. Stock Manager — reconciliations, backdated postings, cancellations and amendments, the settings pages, lateral and allocation approvals. Held by named individuals, not by convenience.
3. The exception roles — frozen-stock editing, over-delivery tolerance, the recall freeze authority: each a register row with its named holders.
4. The separations — the keeper does not approve their own adjustments (module 1); the counter does not enter their own counts (module 4); the preparer and reviewer split on value-moving documents (module 2).

2. The quarterly recertification. Per the Sysadmin track's procedure, applied to stock: the matrix's stock rows walked against the live role assignments; leavers and movers confirmed removed (the HR lifecycle feed); exception-role holders re-confirmed by the owner; the recertification dated in the register.

3. The adjustments read. Monthly, network-wide: every Stock Reconciliation and every Material Issue above the de-minimis band, listed with its author, approver, warehouse, and value. The read answers two questions:

1. Concentration — adjustment powers should resolve to a small set of named people. The healthy result is that the month's adjustments across the network trace to the named Stock Manager holders and no one else; an unfamiliar name on the list is a permission drift found by reading rather than by incident.
2. Pattern — the same warehouse, item class, or author recurring across months joins module 4's pattern file. The read is data assembly; conclusions and responses belong to the owner per the standing rule.

4. The access boundary cases, stated. Temporary elevation (the deputy covering leave) is granted by the procedure with an expiry date and removed on return — the recertification checks expired grants specifically. Shared logins are prohibited for stock roles without exception: every adjustment must resolve to an individual, because the separations of point 1 are meaningless between accounts two people share. Service and integration accounts that post stock documents are register rows like human holders, with their scopes stated.

The recertification, and why it is calendared rather than triggered. Access accumulates: a temporary grant for a cover period, a power given during a remediation, a role assigned at go-live to somebody now doing something else. None of it removes itself, and nobody notices a permission that is merely unused. Walking the matrix against who actually does what, on a date, is the only reliable way it gets cleaned — and the adjustments read is what shows whether the powers granted are being exercised at all.

The adjustments read in one line. Who posted reconciliations and backdated entries this month, how many, and against which warehouses. It is a short list at a healthy business, and it is the read that makes the Stock Manager role answerable rather than merely named.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Records and handover
lessons.html:
The track's procedures generate evidence. This chapter is where it files, how long it is kept, and how a role hands over.

1. The filing map. One location per file class, named in the procedure:

1. Count files — per count: signed sheets, the variance report, investigation notes, the posted reconciliation reference (module 4). Filed per warehouse per date.
2. Recall files — per event or drill: the notice, timings, snapshot, transfers, trace, disposition (module 3, Chapter 7).
3. Remediation files — per project: scope, before-state, batches, verification (module 5's discipline).
4. Review packs — monthly: the health page with its decision list and worksheets (modules 6-7); the run notes and allocation worksheets (module 6).
5. The register and matrix — current versions plus superseded rows (Chapters 3, 5).

2. Retention. Stock records support financial reporting and, for regulated goods, compliance obligations: retention follows the longer of the accounting retention the Accounts track sets and the regulatory retention the compliance owner sets, per record class, written in the filing map. Nothing in the map is deleted informally; disposal at end of retention is itself a logged action per the site's records procedure.

3. The one-lookup standard, restated as a test. Any question about any stock event — a count adjustment two years back, a recall's customer list, an allocation's arithmetic — is answerable from one file location in one sitting. The quarterly test: the stock manager picks three past events and retrieves each file; a retrieval that requires reconstruction from memory or from multiple locations is a filing-map correction.

4. The handover file. Per role, maintained current rather than written at departure:

1. The stock manager's file — the register, the matrix section, the review calendar, the run procedure (module 6's closing notes), the open items list (current investigations, in-flight remediations, pending delistings).
2. The keeper's file per warehouse — the custody row, the count cadence, the site's procedures, the current exceptions.
3. The standard: a competent successor operates the role from the file within a week, with questions but without reconstruction. Chapter 8's absence test is this standard, tested by an absence rather than a departure.

5. The records read. Riding the quarterly recertification: the filing map walked, the retrieval test run, the handover files confirmed current (the open-items lists dated within the quarter). Records maintenance is scheduled work; records reconstructed at need are the expensive alternative the schedule exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Multi-company structure
lessons.html:
Where the site runs more than one legal entity, stock structure follows the legal boundary. This chapter is the rules.

1. Per-company structure. Each company holds its own warehouse tree from its own root (module 1, Chapter 3), its own default wiring, and its own settings postures where the system scopes them per company. The control register carries per-company rows where postures differ, and the annual settings review walks each company.

2. The item register decision. Items are shared across companies on one register, with per-company rows carrying the defaults (module 1's Item Defaults per company) and the accounts derivations per the Accounts track. The decision recorded in the register: which item classes both companies trade, and which are single-company by policy — because a shared register with unshared intentions produces items ordered by the wrong entity through an unconsidered default.

3. Inter-company stock movement. Stock crossing the legal boundary is a sale and a purchase, not a transfer:

1. The documents — the selling company's Delivery Note and Sales Invoice; the buying company's Purchase Receipt and Purchase Invoice; the inter-company document links where the site's configuration creates the counterpart automatically. The Accounts track owns the pricing and settlement rules; this module's rule is the stock side: an internal Material Transfer never crosses a company boundary.
2. Why — a cross-company transfer moves value between legal entities with no sale recorded: both companies' accounts misstate, and the correction is an accounting remediation. The system's company scoping refuses the direct case; the rule exists for the indirect ones (the shared building's informal handover between two entities' shelves).
3. The shared-building procedure — where two entities occupy one site (module 1, Chapter 3), the physical segregation is explicit, the keepers know which shelves belong to which company's warehouses, and any goods crossing between them move by the inter-company documents on the same day the goods move.

4. Identity and counts across companies. Batch and serial records follow the item register's sharing: a batch received by one company and sold to the other carries through both companies' documents, and a recall trace (module 3) runs across both entities' delivery records — the recall file notes the entity per holding. Counts run per company per warehouse; the accuracy metric reports per company; and the tie-out (module 5) runs per company's stock accounts, because each entity's balance sheet stands alone.

5. The multi-company read. Quarterly: inter-company stock document pairs reconciled (every despatch matched to its counterpart receipt and both invoices); unmatched pairs investigated as the month-end items they are. The read belongs to the accounts close checklist; the stock function's part is the document discipline that keeps the read short.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the structural year and the absence test
lessons.html:
This chapter runs Chapters 2-7 through HealthTrade's structural year. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the settings walk with the MD (Chapter 2). The first annual review walks Stock Settings against the draft register: the negative-stock posture confirmed off (module 5's remediation recorded as its reason); the freeze controls aligned to the close calendar with the rolling-days rule enforcing same-day posting; the over-delivery tolerance reduced to the policy figure with the exception role named; reorder automation confirmed on only for the sites whose levels were set from data. The walk's output is the register's first complete revision — every posture with an owner, a reason, and a review date.

Step 2 — the adjustments read establishes its baseline (Chapter 5). The first monthly read lists the network's reconciliations and banded issues: every adjustment traces to two names network-wide — the named Stock Manager holders — and no one else. The result files as the baseline; the read thereafter is a five-minute confirmation that the concentration holds, and one quarter's list showing a third name resolves to a documented temporary elevation with its expiry date, verified against the register.

Step 3 — the creation gate catches its case (Chapter 4). A new-item request duplicates an existing line under a supplier's alternative product name; the gate's duplicate search matches on the barcode and stops the creation. The counterfactual files in the training note: the duplicate would have split the item's history, doubled its reorder arithmetic, and produced count disagreements at every site stocking both records.

Step 4 — the retirement flow at scale (Chapter 4). The range review's delisting batch — 60 delistings — executes through the four-step flow: stock resolved through module 7's lanes, reorder rows removed at every site, price lists cleared, each item disabled at zero. Execution status tracks on the review list until all sixty close; two items found with residual balances mid-flow are returned to the lanes rather than disabled over stock.

Step 5 — the absence test (Chapters 3-6). The founder — the business's most experienced stock decision-maker — is abroad for three weeks. The structural layer's test:

1. The weekly replenishment runs execute from the run procedure and closing notes; the deputy approves per the documented ladder.
2. The two-name controls hold for the twenty-one days — the temporary elevation granted by procedure with its expiry, and removed on return, verified at the next recertification.
3. One incident — a transit shortfall — is resolved entirely from the documents: the despatch entry, the receiving count, the investigation lane, the closure under the ladder, per module 2's procedure. The resolution requires no individual's recollection: the file answers every question the investigation asks.
4. The monthly health page compiles on schedule by the deputy from the documented method.

The test's conclusion files with the register review: the stock function operates from its structure. The findings list is short — one procedure step ambiguously worded, corrected; one handover file's open-items list found a month stale, corrected and added to the quarterly records read.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review, the module rule, and the track recap
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in the structural layer, the module rule, and the track's eight rules.

Error 1 — settings nobody owns. Symptom: postures set at implementation and never reviewed; departures nobody can explain. Correction: the settings walk run, the register built. Prevention: the annual review with the owner, dated in the register.

Error 2 — the register that trails the system. Symptom: control changes made but not recorded; the register describing a past configuration. Correction: the quarterly confirmation against the live system. Prevention: the rule that a change is not complete until its row is updated.

Error 3 — items created around the gate. Symptom: duplicates splitting histories; identity flags missing at first receipt; defaults absent. Correction: duplicates merged by remediation; flags and defaults completed. Prevention: the creation gate as the only entry path, with the monthly sample read.

Error 4 — deletion as retirement. Symptom: items deleted with history referencing them; reports and documents breaking. Correction: records restored per the incident lane. Prevention: the retirement flow — lanes, disconnection, disabled at zero, never deleted.

Error 5 — adjustment powers spreading. Symptom: reconciliations posted by names outside the matrix; separations collapsing quietly. Correction: the permissions corrected; the affected adjustments reviewed. Prevention: the monthly adjustments read against the named holders, and the quarterly recertification.

Error 6 — the transfer across the company boundary. Symptom: stock moved between entities without sale documents; both balance sheets misstating. Correction: the accounting remediation with the inter-company documents entered. Prevention: the rule that an internal transfer never crosses a company boundary, and the quarterly pair reconciliation.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the Stock Settings walk with the recommended postures and the annual review; maintain the control register with its row format and quarterly confirmation; run the item lifecycle — the creation gate, change governance, the four-step retirement flow, and the lifecycle reads; operate the consolidated matrix, the recertification, and the adjustments read with its concentration and pattern questions; apply the filing map, retention rules, the retrieval test, and the handover files; and configure multi-company structure with the inter-company document rule.

Module rule 8: the stock function runs on structure — settings decided, registered, and reviewed annually; items entering by gate and leaving by the retirement flow; powers named, separated, recertified, and read monthly; evidence filed to the one-lookup standard; and the whole operable through any absence from its documents alone.

The track's eight rules.

1. A warehouse is a named accountability unit — designed into a shallow tree by written convention, stocked only at leaf level, wired into defaults once and verified, held by a named keeper, and changed only by document.
2. Every internal movement is a Stock Entry with its purpose — transfers received against what physically arrived, issues and receipts carrying reason, account, evidence, and approval, repacks held to their register, and every entry posted on its honest date.
3. Identity travels with the stock — captured once from the physical goods at the dock, named on every movement and confirmed at every handover, expiries read on their horizons, and any batch freezable and locatable across the network in minutes.
4. A count proves custody — blind sheets counted and entered by separate hands, variances recounted then investigated before anything posts, adjustments approved by band with their evidence attached, and accuracy measured on a cycle that costs minutes a day.
5. Value follows the documents — rates born at their four doors and nowhere else, landed costs on every named consignment, methods set by recorded policy, the stock ledger tied to the accounts at zero every month, backdating carrying its repost cost consciously, and every strange rate stopped at entry.
6. The network replenishes by procedure — requests reasoned on projected quantities, a weekly run with reasoned adjustments, scarcity allocated by written rule and shown as arithmetic, branches opened by transfer and reviewed weekly for ninety days, and every flow through the standard documents with a recorded reason.
7. Stock health is read on schedule and resolved by lane — aging and movement compiled monthly by the documented method, every listed item assigned a lane with its document, rebalancing before markdown and write-off last, findings routed upstream, and the whole reported on one page whose first figure is the accuracy of the records it stands on.
8. The stock function runs on structure — settings registered and reviewed, items by gate and retirement flow, powers named and read, evidence to the one-lookup standard, and the whole operable through any absence from its documents alone.
